utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Presiding Judge and good morning to Your Honours. Your Honour, I will respond to the legal arguments raised by the appellants in their respective briefs, and during the oral submissions made by several of the appellants' counsel in relation to the legal elements of joint criminal enterprise. The challenges to the factual findings of the application of this form of liability will be addressed by the prosecuting team in response to each of the appellants' briefs. Your Honour, briefly, the Trial Chamber found that the camp, the Omarska camp, was established by the Serb authorities in Prijedor municipality on or about 27th of May, 1992. They will call Omarska and the other camps were called collection centres. And the purpose was to identify individuals suspected of collaborating with the opposition. Omarska camp was dismantled at the end of August due to pressure exerted from the international community. The individuals establishing and running the camps were all Serbs. The Crisis Staff, including Simo Drljaca, established the camp. The camp commander was undisputably Zeljko Meakic. It was undisputed at trial. Security and sentry posts were manned by men from the army and the Omarska Territorial Defence. There were interrogators, there were 30 guards from the Omarska police station, there were people in charge of logistics and mines, management personnel, which had about 35 staff members. This collection centre detained and interrogated not only men of military age, that is, between the ages of 16 and 60, but also older men and some women, about 36 women. At the conclusion of its work sometime in August 1992, the Trial Chamber found that a vast number of the non-Serb men and women, the detainees, were killed, maimed, tortured, raped, and generally mistreated. Three of the appellants were from the Omarska police station. Kvocka was the senior police officer. Prcac was a retired crime technician from the station, and Radic was a police officer assigned to the Ljubija police station. When assigned to work at the camp, each individual took on specific roles and functions. The issue the Trial Chamber had to resolve at trial was why and how is an individual performing seemingly ordinary tasks in an extraordinary place like the Omarska camp liable for the systematic crimes perpetrated by other individuals. The concept of collective criminality, Your Honour, is not new to the Tribunal's jurisprudence. The legality of this mode of liability that the Trial Chamber has applied to the facts of this case is no longer controversial in light of the Appeals Chamber's own judgements and decisions in Tadic, Vasiljevic, Krnojelac, and the Ojdanic decision dated 21st of May, 2003. Essentially, Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber has accepted that there are three categories of cases falling within the concept of joint criminal liability or joint criminal enterprise, JCE. The most relevant and appropriate category applicable to this case is the second category or the second variant, which I will call JCE 2. The Appeals Chamber has accepted that the elements relevant and common to all the categories of JCA, there are basically three. The Prosecution need to prove a plurality of persons. There has to be the existence of a common plan, design, or purpose which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute. The third element is the participation of an accused in the common design. Now, the Appeals Chamber has accepted a broad category of participation which included -- which involved the perpetration of one of the crimes provided for in the Statute or in the form of assistance in or contribution to the execution of the common plan or purpose. So the emphasis is contribution to the execution of the common plan or purpose. With regard to the mens rea element for JCE 2, the Trial Chamber adopted Tadic, and this is in line also with the recent Krnojelac Appeals Chamber judgement. The mens rea is sharing the intent of the system which presupposes the knowledge of the system of ill-treatment and intent to further the concerted system of ill-treatment. Your Honour, in the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber was very careful to circumscribe the legal discussion on the mode of liability to the facts at hand and in relation to the participation of lower-level or mid-level actors in the criminal enterprise. Not low-level actors, Your Honour, lower-level actors. The Trial Chamber recognised and acknowledged that the appellants did not organise the camps, they did not orchestrate the campaign of violence within the camp, but that they were key players who had participated in the functioning of the camp operating as a criminal enterprise. What the Trial Chamber did was that they made a very careful and studied analysis not only of established Tribunal jurisprudence, such as the Tadic Appeals Chamber's judgement, but they also conducted an extensive survey of post-World War II cases, also World War II cases. The analysis can be found from pages 71 to 88 of the judgement. What was the Trial Chamber looking for? The focus of their analysis was the liability of individuals, civilians performing tasks within the ordinary course of their employment and who often did not physically perpetrate the crimes committed by the organisation that they were working in: Medical personnel; industrialists who supplied poisoned gas to concentration camps; persons who work in an administrative facility where children were abandoned and died. In relation to camp cases, the Trial Chamber concluded that those who did not physically perpetrate a crime can be found guilty if crimes falling within the common plan, if they remain -- can be found guilty of crimes falling within the common plan if they remain in their assigned positions and continue participating in the functioning of the camp if the participation is significant in position or effect. And that can be found at paragraphs 284 and 310 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber concluded at paragraph 282 it is possible, then, to trace in the jurisprudence of the concentration-camp cases a theory in which criminal liability will attach to staff members of the camps who have knowledge of the crimes being committed there unless - unless - their role is not administrative or supervisory or interwoven with illegality; or unless, despite having a significant status their actual contribution to the enterprise was insignificant. Therefore, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber found that in order to be criminally liable as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, an accused must have carried out acts that substantially assisted or significantly affected the furtherance of the goals of the enterprise with the knowledge that his or her acts or omissions facilitated the crime through the enterprise. There is at this point in time, Your Honour, a point that we wish to highlight which is not in the briefs. It is our submission that although the Trial Chamber was correct in its factual analysis and in concluding on the facts that the appellants' contributions were significant, under Tribunal law, under existing Tribunal law, and particularly in light of the recent Krnojelac Appeals Chamber's judgement dealing with the systematic form of JCE, the Prosecution need only show that the participant contributes to the execution of the common plan. That is the clear requirement from the Tadic Appeals Chamber's judgement. Therefore, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the participation must be significant is additional, over and above the requirements set out by the Appeals Chamber in all of its judgements. If the Appeals Chamber is of the view that the Trial Chamber did apply an additional requirement, we submit, however, that this in no way prejudiced the appellant, in no way occasioned a miscarriage of justice, and in fact, what it does is to strengthen the findings of the Trial Chamber. Applying the legal elements to the case at hand, the Trial Chamber concluded that the crimes in the Omarska camp were committed by a plurality of persons, indeed, they could only have been committed by a plurality of persons. The establishment, the organisation, the functioning of the camp required the participation of many individuals, playing a variety of roles and performing different functions of lesser or greater degrees of importance. The JCE pervading the camp was the intent to persecute and subjugate the non-Serb detainees. The persecution was committed through crimes such as murder, torture, and rape and by various means, such as mental and physical violence, and inhumane conditions of detention. We submit, Your Honour, that apart from the additional requirement that I have highlighted, the Trial Chamber's legal findings correctly set out the basis of criminal responsibility of the appellants. Your Honour, I would like to turn to more specific arguments raised by two of the appellants, Zigic and Kvocka, Your Honour. They have sought refuge in the contentions that they should not have been found liable for crimes committed in their absences. Zigic also added that this form of liability is completely unnatural, as he was convicted of crimes even when he was in prison, when he was sleeping or when he was physically out of the camp. Kvocka claims that since he was on official leave from the camp on two occasions, he should not have been found liable for crimes committed during those times as well. Related to this issue, Your Honour, raised by all the appellants is the scope of the contribution to the JCE, which is required to attract liability. As I've said, Your Honour, my colleagues will address the challenges to the legal -- to the factual findings but I will deal with the general legal principles now. It must be highlighted that there is a 98 bis decision by the Trial Chamber in this case and which is set out at paragraph 349 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber decided, Your Honour, that the accused will not be responsible for crimes committed before he arrived at the camp to take up his employment and after the accused leaves the camp. All parties accepted that decision. We proceeded with a trial on that basis. However, in the -- in our response brief, Your Honour, we have stated our positions on the Trial Chamber's decision to impose temporal cuts to an accused's liability in light of the continuing nature of the crimes committed in Omarska. We submit that this is a legal issue of general importance, to the Tribunal's jurisprudence and we invite the Appeals Chamber to consider our submissions and to provide us with some guidance on this issue, Your Honour. The arguments are set out from paragraphs 3.4 onwards. I do not propose to touch on this issue but I'd be more than happy to assist the Court with any clarifications or elaborations. In response to specific arguments, there are a few points that I wish to make. Firstly, the basis of the appellants' liability is the significance of their contributions to the common design, to the system of ill-treatment, and I must emphasise again, Your Honour, the element common plan or design or purpose amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute. Therefore, Your Honour, it follows that in a systemic form of JCE, the crimes are relevant to establish the existence of the system of persecution or subjugation in this case. Third, the significance of a participant's contribution is not necessarily dependent on the duration of the contributions. It is one of the -- a number of relevant considerations. It is not necessary for the Prosecution to show, for example, that the appellants intended to persecute the non-Serbs at the camp every minute of their waking hours. Most of the staff who worked at the camp worked normal working hours or in 12-hour shifts. I can cite you some references to the trial record. The evidence of Milenko Jasnic at transcript page 11533 and the evidence of DD/10, transcript page T1066. These individuals, they went home after their work was done. They get to leave camp. The arguments that the appellants cannot be held liable for crimes not committed every time they stepped out of the camp fully intending to return to the camp to continue with their job, it militates against the systemic theory of liability and must be rejected. Therefore, Your Honour, for example, at paragraph 399, although the Trial Chamber noted that Kvocka was physically working at the camp for approximately 17 days or 20 shifts, the amount is not insubstantial, considering the litany of crimes that were committed on a daily, even hourly, basis. The Trial Chamber found in relation to Radic that despite knowledge of abusive treatment, he continued working in the camp for nearly three months. Finally, Your Honour, liability is not excluded. It is not truncated even if persons enter and leave the system. The Appellant Zigic was correctly held liable not because of the duration of his contributions but because he contributed in the most direct way possible. By committing very serious crimes, he contributed to the system of persecution, which consisted of the commission of crimes. Without the crimes, there would be no system of persecution; without the likes of Zigic, there would be no crimes. Fourth, Your Honour, in relation to knowledge of the system, the Trial Chamber correctly observed the participant did not know of each crime committed. Knowledge that a wide variety of crimes committed within a system, the criminal nature of the system, the discriminatory practices and policies is sufficient. The Belsen trial also supports that conclusion. The judge advocate in that case in summarising the evidence stated that the case for the Prosecution was that all the accused employed on the staff knew that a system and a course of conduct was in force and that in one way or another, in furtherance of a common agreement to run the camp in a brutal way, all those people were taking part in that course of conduct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Personal involvement with crimes is also -- or physical presence at the time of the commission of the crimes are not prerequisites when determining significance of the contribution of the accused to the system. Fifth, Your Honour, a position of authority in the sense that the accused has command responsibility or control over the perpetrators as suggested by counsel is not a prerequisite. It's not to be found anywhere in the jurisprudence. The reliance on Krnojelac for this proposition is also misplaced. In paragraph 269 of the judgement, Your Honour, I would highlight the Trial Chamber's reliance on the Dachau and the Belsen concentration camp cases and noted that the accused held some position of authority not formally prescribed. Even camp inmates were given authority over others. Having analysed the jurisprudence, the Trial Chamber concluded that these cases, the World War II cases, Your Honour, seemingly establish a rebuttable presumption that holding an executive, administrative or protective role in the camp constitutes general participation. This is consist with the modern approach applied by the Appeals Chamber in Krnojelac, for example, where his position as the camp commander raised a very strong inference that he was aware of the systemic crimes and that he agreed to the system. Therefore, the position of authority or influence of the accused is just one of the relevant indicators. Sixth, Your Honour, the fact that a few crimes fell outside the period of employment, for example, in the case of Kvocka where we have analysed some of the murders and the tortures and, quite clearly, some of the murders occurred after Kvocka had left the camp. We have identified about three murders. We submit that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, to the interpreters. We submit that this does not extentuate the extent of his liability. It does not in a material way affect his sentence in any significant matter or at all. And that is because the basis of his liability was his contributions to the system. The crimes were the means to achieve and perpetuate the prosecutory system. Count 1 of the amended indictment essentially charged Kvocka with involvement in the persecution of non-Serbs on discriminatory grounds using the following means: Murder, torture, torture and beating, sexual assault, and rape. It is sufficient for the Trial Chamber to find that one or a few of these means were committed during Kvocka's stay to ascribe liability to him as a participant in the JCE. Therefore, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber's approach of attaching liability from the perspective of significant contribution, rather than an approach of seeking to establish precise links to the individual crimes or individual perpetrators, is the correct one; and in fact it finds support in the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber's judgement, for example, at paragraph 97 of that judgement. The crimes committed in Omarska were of a continuing, pervasive nature. In light of their frequency, the scale and magnitude, the Trial Chamber rejected Kvocka's argument that he was only working on 20 shifts in the camp, days working in Omarska, concluding that this amount of time is not insubstantial given the frequency and the scale of the crimes and given his own significant contributions when he was there. In relation to the scope of contribution, Your Honours, first, the participation in the enterprise must be significant. What is significant? An act or omission that makes an enterprise sufficient or effective; participation that enables the system to run smoothly without disruption. Physical or direct perpetration of serious crimes that advances the goal of the criminal enterprise will definitely constitute a significant contribution. In the Dachau trial it was observed that the culpability of an accused for participation in a common criminal design could arise when the accused's duties were, A, they were such as to constitute in themselves an execution or administration of the system. That would be sufficient to make the accused guilty of participation in the -- in that system; or B, were not in themselves illegal or interwoven with illegality but were performed in an illegal manner. Now, this second category makes it clear that any individual, regardless of his position within the camp's hierarchy, can be held liable as a participant in a system of ill-treatment if he or she performs her job in an illegal manner. Secondly, the significance of a participant's contribution determines not only liability but also liability either as a co-perpetrator or an aider and abetter, particularly in the case of lower-level perpetrators. A person who does not commit crimes but directs the overall operations, thus ensuring perpetuation of his crimes offers significant contribution. In the case of Krnojelac, he was the camp warden. The Trial Chamber found Krstic, in the case of Prosecutor and Krstic, guilty of co-perpetrator of a joint criminal enterprise because his participation of playing a key coordinating role is of an extremely significant nature and at the leadership level. And that's at paragraph 642 of the Krstic judgement. The contributions of, for example, Zigic, were significant because he contributed directly to the core of the common design which is the common plan to persecute against the non-Serbs. Similarly with appellant Radic; his contribution straddled both categories, commission of egregious acts and in fulfilling his duties as the shift-guard leader, thereby ensuring that the system functioned efficiently. Kvocka's and Prcac's role provided a valuable service to the camp. Their administrative duties substantially contributed to the execution of the persecutory system. Your Honour, it is useful to know the Einsatzgruppen case which distinguished between significant and insignificant contributions to the JCE, taking into account the nature of the duties performed by the accused and also whether the accused was in a position to protest or influence the criminal activities. In the case of Ruehl, from the same case, the Einsatzgruppen case, it was concluded, Your Honour, that although Ruehl had knowledge of some of the illegal operations of the unit that effected the execution of Jews, it was not established that he was in a position to control, prevent, or modify the severity of its programme although he remained with the organisation for no more than three months and during the entire period took no part in the execution. Nor did his low rank place him automatically into a position where his lack of objection in any way contributed to the success of any executive operation. So he was acquitted of the crimes. But as the Tribunal has correctly pointed out, this is not the case if he was the commander. He would have been liable for the crimes. The Trial Chamber concluded that none of the appellants here fall into the category of humanitarian workers. For example, a doctor who visited the camp at Omarska to assist the detainees, he will not be held liable because his contributions do not further the system of ill-treatment. Perhaps the most important factor to examine, Your Honour, at the end of the day, is the role of the accused vis-a-vis the seriousness and scope of the crimes committed. Third, Your Honour, the significance of participation will also determine the requisite mens rea, whether the participant shares the intent of the enterprise, in the sense that he intended to further the system, or that he merely had knowledge in the sense that he is at the end of the day an aider and abetter to the system. If I may offer an illustration, Your Honour. If an individual was asked to drive his truck into Omarska camp and a truck -- and the bodies at the Omarska camp were loaded on his truck and he drives away to a mass grave, he is of course aware that mass killings had occurred and he knew that he was assisting in the efficient disposal of the bodies; substantial contribution. However, it cannot reasonably be inferred that because he assisted on that one occasion he agreed to the system or actively shared intent. Now, if an individual walks into Omarska camp knowing full well that there is this climate of impunity, that detainees are abused on a daily basis, and on that one occasion maliciously, deliberately, killed a detainee, his contribution is so direct and so significant to advancing the purpose of the system that the only reasonable inference is that he agreed with the system, he shared the goals of the system, and that he must be liable as a co-perpetrator. We submit, Your Honour, that the Trial Chamber's analysis and conclusions on the legal criteria in determining the appellants' liability are unimpeachable and must be upheld. The appellants' challenges to these findings must be rejected. Your Honour, I will now turn to the appellants' collective argument that they lacked the requisite mens rea applicable to this mode of liability. Kvocka claimed, for example, that he lacked any shared intent. He said that he was obliged by his superiors and professions to carry out his duties. Radic submitted that he acted in accordance with the structure of his personality, that he was merely obeying orders and that he had no discriminatory intent. Prcac argued that he acted -- he was at the camp under threat and duress. All these arguments must be dismissed. Basically they're saying that they should not have been found liable as a co-perpetrator due to all these reasons. The factual aspects of the argument will be addressed, Your Honour, later, but the legal requirement of the mens rea will be addressed now. The Trial Chamber made a factual finding that all four appellants shared the discriminatory intent of the common enterprise in light of their knowing and substantial participation in the system of persecution. The Trial Chamber's legal findings are correct; they are consistent with the Appeal Chamber's judgements and decisions. First, Your Honour, precise knowledge of each and every crime committed is not required. Second, the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber's judgement at paragraph 100 has held that shared criminal intent does not require the co-perpetrator's personal satisfaction or enthusiasm or his personal initiative in contributing to the system. Personal motives of the perpetrator must be distinguished from intent, motive is not relevant to establishing liability. Third, at paragraph 96 of its judgement, the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber clarified the interplay between knowledge and intent, explaining that in a systemic form of JCE, the intent, that is, the shared intent of the participants, not necessarily the direct perpetrators, presupposes two things: Knowledge of the system and intent to further the system of ill-treatment. Using this criteria what needs to be proved is their involvement in the system, not necessarily to establish an agreement between all the participants. Therefore, Your Honour, from the -- in Krnojelac all that was required was that he knew of the system and agreed to it, that is, the system, and not with individual perpetrators or the commission of individual crimes. Therefore, intent in JCE 2 exists where an accused is aware of the nature of the intent of other co-perpetrators and guided by such knowledge voluntarily contributes to that common design, meaning to make that contribution. In conclusion, Your Honour, if an accused acted with intent, it is immaterial that the accused's motive was to follow orders, or do his duty, or to avoid possible negative consequences. An indifferent, unenthusiastic, reluctant co-perpetrator is still a co-perpetrator, provided he or she has contributed in a significant way to the JCE and that he or she shares the common criminal intent. The appellants' arguments to the mens rea element must also be rejected. Your Honour, turning to my last final point on the -- on JCE, this relates to the issue of abandonment, disengagement or withdrawal from the system. This issue has arisen because -- partly because Kvocka argues that he should not have been found liable for crimes committed during periods of absences and that he was unable to leave the camp because it might affect his job. Prcac appears to argue that he was mobilised under threat and duress and that he was appointed to work at the Omarska camp. Radic argues that he feared his sons would be sent to the front line if he had refused. In other words, most of the appellants have argued that they had very little choice to work at the camp. In its judgement at paragraph 709, the Trial Chamber concluded the defendants worked in the camp from between 17 days to three months. If during this time they had relentlessly sought to improve the conditions, prevent crimes, alleviate the suffering, they would likely escape liability for participating in the persecutory scheme. The Trial Chamber found on the facts of this case none of the defendants fits the bill. The Trial Chamber has therefore addressed the very same issue raised, whether there were circumstances relevant to either extenuate liability or mitigate culpability. Circumstances where an individual could effectively disengage or withdraw from an enterprise which was clearly illegal, thus possibly escaping liability. The Trial Chamber in Krnojelac indicated that resignation from a job that places one in such a system is the only way to disengage or withdraw from the system. Some of the more pertinent questions to ask: Was the accused in a position to refuse the work assignment? Was there a risk that the accused would suffer, for instance, imprisonment if he refused the assignment? Is there evidence that -- of others leaving the system without any adverse consequences? In rejecting Kvocka's complaints also made at trial, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 402 that there is no evidence that indicates that Serbs who worked in the camp who assisted or tried to improve the conditions of the detainees were punished. Your Honour, I must point out that in the brief, in the response brief, the Prosecution has offered a comparative analysis of domestic jurisprudence to illustrate the general principles underlying the concept of withdrawal or abandonment, but I must point out that their applicability depends on the nature of the crime. For example, the US model Penal Code and the English jurisprudence that we have cited pertain to specific crimes, a single crime, that is, and averting the completion of those crimes of conduct amounting to -- and if there is a successful renunciation, that might amount to mitigation; for example, in the cases of attempt. In this present case, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber recognised the continuing nature of the crimes. Because of the continuing nature of the systemic crimes, Your Honour, the notion of completion of a crime does not necessarily arise. However, the cases we have cited offer some guidance consistent with the Trial Chamber's observations on withdrawal from the system. For example, in the German law, for the affirmative defence of renunciation, it is required that the actor, after conspiring to commit a crime, thwarted the success of the conspiracy, under circumstances manifesting a complete and voluntary renunciation of his criminal purpose. The Statute of the ICC also contains an express provision on abandonment of a criminal attempt, and thus in Article 25(3)(f), which relieved the actor of any liability for the attempt if that person completely and voluntarily gave up the criminal purpose. The question is do the appellants' own personal motivations and reasons for staying at the camp amount to a recognised legal defence? We submit that the reasons for Kvocka's absences do not amount to effective disengagement or abandonment by him of the joint criminal enterprise. He was on official leave and sick leave from the 2nd to the 6th of June, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 16th to the 19th of June respectively, and during his leave, he spent time with his wife's family. As for the sick -- Your Honour, yes.

Your Honour, we submit that the periods of absences that Kvocka had taken were well within the usual terms of employment. When Kvocka returned to the camp, he continued to be actively involved with his duties. He was not dismissed. He didn't lose his job. But he was transferred to another police station at Tukovi. He did not leave the camp on his own initiative. He did not abandon the camp on his own initiative. There was no evidence, Your Honour, that he did anything to precipitate his departure from the camp. On the contrary, he made it very clear that if he had a choice, he would have continued working at the camp. The Trial Chamber concluded at paragraph 403 even if a knowing participant in a criminal enterprise was unwilling to resign because he would prejudice his career or he feared he would be spent to the front lines, imprisoned or punished, the Trial Chamber emphasises that this is not an excuse or a defence to liability for participating in war crimes and crimes against humanity. Kvocka's only excuse is that he feared he would lose his job. Presumably because of this, he knowingly participated in a system where hundreds of detainees lost their lives. Could the appellants, Your Honour, have chosen not to work in an organisation that was so obviously criminal? Yes, they could. Radic testified in court that nothing happened to guards who did not turn up for work. Some went to their farms, others went swimming. He said it depends on the individual and how conscientious he was in performing his job at Omarska. That's at transcript page 11297. Another witness, Nada Markovska, she was ordered to work at Omarska as a typist. She went all the way and saw Simo Drljaca complain about the work being too hard and was permitted to leave the camp. That's at transcript page 7782. DD/10 left at her own initiative, complained to Drljaca and confronted him about conditions at the camp and as she puts it, she didn't lose her head. That's at transcript page T10699. And then Defence witnesses testified that the organisation in the camp was so lax that guards failed to show up for work without any repercussions. The only reasonable conclusion open to the Trial Chamber was that the appellants were knowing and they were willing participants of the persecutory system and that they did nothing to disengage themselves from the system. Having heard the appellants, Your Honour, their complaints remain devoid of merit and must be dismissed. Your Honour, if I could conclude with some observations from the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber correctly concluded that the primary work of the staff individuals working at Omarska camp was to ensure that the prisoners stayed in their miserable conditions and the camp system functioned without disruption or hassle. If we remove the Zigics, the Prcacs, the Kvockas, the Radics, the administrators, the guards, the interrogators, the typists from the camp, the camp would not have run its course effectively and people would not have died needlessly. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 709 without their guarding function, without the role they played in maintaining the efficient and continuous functioning of the camp there could have been no camp at all. For all these reasons, Your Honour, and reasons which will be highlighted by the Prosecution team, the Trial Chamber correctly concluded on the law and on the facts that the appellants were liable for the crimes committed in Omarska as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. The appellants' common ground of appeal must therefore be rejected. Your Honour, that concludes my submissions on the common ground of appeal. If I'm not able to assist the Court in any way, I will turn to my response to Kvocka's grounds of appeal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're not through? You will speak further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: I have completed my submissions on common ground of appeal and I will respond to grounds of appeal raised by the Appellant Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think our sense is that you should be allowed to proceed and to conclude your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Appellant Kvocka has raised a number of alleged errors in his Appeal Brief. I will, however, respond to four, perhaps five points raised in his oral submissions yesterday. The first point relates to the admissibility of an OTP interview statements which Kvocka has given to the OTP. It is marked as Exhibit P3/103 at trial. Kvocka claims, Your Honour, that because he chose to testify in court the transcript of this interview should not have been admitted or relied upon by the Trial Chamber. His only reasoning is a reference to the principle of directness. I don't propose to dwell on this issue long because we do not accept that this issue is unresolved or that there is an ambiguity in the Rules governing admissibility of an accused's statement or that there was an error of law. There is no dispute, Your Honour, that the statement was recorded in accordance with the procedure set out in the Rules, Rules 42, 43, and 63. And most importantly, yesterday Judge Mumba, I believe, clarified with counsel that Kvocka was cautioned that any statement he made may be used in evidence, and that is not disputed either. Your Honour, the statement was used in the course of cross-examining Kvocka, and parts were relied by the Prosecution as assertions of truth. The Trial Chamber also referred to the statement in the judgement. In the law and practice of the Tribunal, Your Honour, there is a difference between the use that can be made of a witness statement and that of an accused. I must also point out that the exact same challenge that the appellant has raised today was in fact raised at trial and resolved by the Trial Chamber in its decision dated 16th of March, 2001. The appellant has made no reference to this decision and has not made any submission as to why the Trial Chamber committed an error of law in its decision in admitting the statement. The Trial Chamber admitted the statement because the Rules provided for it, Rule 42, and was satisfied that all the measures protecting the rights of the accused were complied with, and concluded that under the circumstances, omission of the document at issue which is evidently relevant and has probative value cannot be considered contrary to the demands for a fair trial and that the Judges shall assess the weight to be given to this evidence at the appropriate time. In other words, the statement, Your Honour, was treated like any other evidence, regard being given to its probative value and weight, except for the fact that its admissibility was governed by specific provisions in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And I have cited in the brief as well, Your Honour, a judgement, the Celebici appeals judgement which specifically rule that a Trial Chamber is entitled to rely on the substance of such statements to convict if voluntarily made. That's in the case of Music. That's the Celebici appeals judgement paragraph 564. I should also cite a recent Trial Chamber's judgement in Prosecutor and Simic, where the Trial Chamber did use Zaric's and Tadic's OTP interview statements despite their decision to testify in court. The jurisprudence is clear. The Rules are not unambiguous [sic]. The statement was -- the Trial Chamber was entitled to admit and use the statement because it was probative, and the Trial Chamber exercised its discretion in attaching the relevant weight to it. No error has been shown by the appellant. This argument must be rejected. The second legal error, or factual error, that the appellant has raised relates to the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Kvocka had occupied a position similar to a de facto position of authority and influence at Omarska camp. There are basically four points that I wish to make, Your Honour, very briefly, in relation to this argument. First of all, the Trial Chamber found -- did not find that Kvocka was a deputy commander. He found that - excuse me, Your Honour - He found that Kvocka was the functional equivalent of a deputy commander, after having assessed his role and his specific duties at the camp. Second, Your Honour, the liability as a participant and a co-perpetrator is not dependent on formalised titles but rather on the contributions that the participant had made to the system. Kvocka also criticised the evidence of several witnesses yesterday in court. He seems to suggest that it was the impression of witnesses that he was the deputy commander and that was all the evidence that the Trial Chamber had relied on. This is clearly not the case. The Trial Chamber had relied on a large number of witnesses who testified that Kvocka occupied a position of authority and influence within the camp. And that's at paragraph 368. Kvocka himself introduced -- he introduced himself as commander and the person in charge to the detainees on at least two occasions. The Trial Chamber also relied on Kvocka's own evidence that he was asked by the commander, Meakic, to help him as senior officer, and that he may have been perceived by junior officers to be one of the superiors because of what he was doing at the camp. Apart from reiterating his defence at trial, the appellant, Your Honour, has not raised any legal error, any factual errors, has not made any references to the Trial Chamber's findings or its reasoning. We submit that this is not sufficient to discharge his obligations, his duty as an appellant. And he has failed to show that the Trial Chamber's conclusions were unreasonable. There is no reason to disturb the Trial Chamber's findings in this regard, Your Honour. The third argument that the appellant has raised relates to his contributions. He argued that his contributions were not significant and therefore he should not be liable as a co-perpetrator. At paragraph 407 of the judgement the Trial Chamber concluded that Kvocka actively contributed to the everyday functioning and maintenance of the camp, including that his conduct made him a co-perpetrator in the JCE, the Trial Chamber said that his contribution to the camp functioning was significant. The Trial Chamber found on the facts that he played a part in the formation of the camp, and this was because Kvocka was one of the first few individuals to arrive at the camp to help set up the security system, and he activated the reserve police guard to come to the camp to act as guards. He was the link between the commander, Meakic, and the police officers serving as guards at the camp. His duties basically pertained to what Meakic told him to do. Meakic was the camp commander and Kvocka acted in his absences. His formal duties were to supervise the reserve police officers who were acting as guards, to oversee the conduct of the police officers and to forward reports to Meakic. One of Kvocka's more interesting tasks was to dictate who was to survive interrogations at the "white house." Witness AK testified that when he was called out of a room by a soldier, Kvocka told the soldier who was talking to him -- he was taking him and Witness AJ, another witness, to the "white house" and he told the soldier: Bring them back here afterwards. The "white house" is notorious. It is well known that detainees who were interrogated in the "white house" would certainly not survive the experience. Zigic and other individuals were eventually convicted of beating Witness AK and Witness AJ, but as per Kvocka's instructions they survived. They were brought back to the room. But Kvocka allowed them to be beaten. Counsel yesterday also referred to another incident involving Nusret Sivac. This incident has been set out in the judgement at paragraph 370(a). Now, what happened was that Kvocka gave instructions to return Nusret Sivac back to Prijedor and instead to arrest his sister, Nusreta Sivac, a woman, a civilian, a judge, a prominent member of the Muslim community. As a result, she was confined in deplorable conditions at the camp, without justification, from 10th of June to 3rd of August. The detention and confinement of a civilian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Rashid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for just a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Private session is ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour. Your Honour, Kvocka also testified that reserve police officers bear the same duties as professional policemen and that the duties of the police officers working in Omarska camp were to prevent prisoners from escaping, to prevent outsiders from entering the camp, and also to prevent attacks on the prisoners. Kvocka and the police officers that he was supervising, therefore, bore responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of the detainees. The Trial Chamber found that Kvocka's insistence that he could not prevent abuse because he did not have sufficient authority was contradicted by the evidence, and there was plenty of evidence. The Trial Chamber found that he could have done far more than what he was doing to mitigate the terrible conditions at the camp. He could have taken steps to prevent unauthorised persons from entering the camps and abusing the detainees. He could have ensured that more detainees received medical treatment. He could have prevented guards and other subordinates from beating or otherwise abusing detainees on arrival in the dining facility or en route to the toilets. He could have done this, because he did offer assistance, but selectively, preferentially, to people that he knew. He did not do so for a vast number of unknowns. Kvocka admitted that when he was there, there were about 2.000 to 2.500 detainees. The Trial Chamber found, Your Honour, that he was a co-perpetrator because, despite having knowledge about the abusive treatment and conditions, he continued to work for at least 17 days at the camp, where the Trial Chamber found he performed his tasks skillfully, efficiently, without complaints. When Kvocka reported for work at the Omarska camp on 29th of May, he saw three to four bodies lying on the grass. He was told that the detainees were shot while attempting to escape during the night. One of them was Muslim policeman Ahid Delic who was quite obviously severely beaten and shot the night before. His only reaction was that, "Well Meakic was with me; he would have seen it. Let him deal with it." Mirsad Alisic testified that about ten days later an elderly gentleman by the name of Nasic was shot dead at the cafeteria by a guard. Kvocka was standing right next to the guard when this happened. Afterwards, Kvocka came to the witness and the only thing he said was, "Why didn't you keep him quiet? " Kvocka was present when bodies covered in blood were loaded onto a truck at the camp. He was responsible for the positioning of the guards at various places in the camp. Why? To prevent detainees from escaping. In holding Kvocka liable as a co-perpetrator of the JCE, the Trial Chamber concluded he was fully aware of the criminal nature of the camp. He was willing to continue in a position of authority and influence. His participation enabled the camp to continue unabated its insidious policies and practices. His continued participation at Omarska sent a message of approval to other participants in the camp's operation. It was a condemnation of the abuses and deplorable conditions there. Your Honour, these are all factual findings arrived at by the Trial Chamber after a careful and studied analysis of all the relevant evidence. Kvocka has not demonstrated that the Trial Chamber erred in the evaluation of the evidence and that the conclusion drawn was so unreasonable in the sense that no reasonable Trial Chamber could arrive at them. Your Honour, I would conclude by observing that Kvocka held the highest level of authority than any of the appellants in this case. Although he was not the architect of the persecutions committed at the camp, he played nothing less than a key role in facilitating and maintaining the functioning of the camp, which allowed the crimes to occur and to continue. For all the reasons set out in the response brief, and we adopt all the reasons that the Trial Chamber has set out in its judgement, we submit that the Trial Chamber committed no error in holding Kvocka responsible for being a member of a joint criminal enterprise at the Omarska camp. I ask that Your Honour uphold the verdict against him and dismiss his appeal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Rashid, I wonder whether you would find it convenient if I invited my colleagues at this point to consider whether they want to ask any questions.

And Radic, Your Honour, was a shift guard leader, also falling within the hierarchy, the command structure of -- that I've just spoken about. I hope I've answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID

That, in our submission, is effective withdrawal, or effective disengagement, that if you leave the system completely and you have no intention of returning to the system. The periods of absences that I was referring to were specifically to the two specific periods of absences arising in Kvocka's case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you very much. Do I understand, then, from your appreciation of the facts of this case you assent to the legal proposition which I pronounced?

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: The legal proposition is that -- could I have the legal proposition again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Your Honours, I would be responding to arguments, the arguments of the appellants in relation to form of the indictment and also in relation to specific grounds that each particular appellant has raised in relation to form of the indictment. Apart from that, I will also be responding to Kvocka's substantive arguments, both factual and legal. I will be responding to rather Prcac's submissions, both factual and legal. Your Honours, the Prosecution needs to make certain general observations with regard to the submissions by my learned colleague. To the extent that a lot of these submissions have in fact been the creatures of hefty generalisations, lacking specific citations, the Prosecution finds itself a bit hamstrung in responding to some of these claims that are very general and very broad. As much as in fact it creates difficulty, however, it is our intention to respond in according terms. In relation to the form of the indictment, the appellants have submitted that they were denied their right to a fair trial and that they were convicted on the basis of an indictment that was fitly vague and that failed to provide material facts supporting the mode of liability under Article 7(1). Concurrent with that submission is a submission that their ability to prepare and present the defence was materially prejudiced and that they were not availed of the requisite factual information to structure the defence in response to the modes of liability under 7(1). And as a corollary of that, that the capacity to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses regarding the precise charges were either compromised or hampered. Specifically, in relation to Prcac and Kvocka, they submit that the amended indictment was defective and that there was no identity between the indictment and the judgement. Prcac specifically argues that the Trial Chamber has in fact gone into the arena, the proverbial arena, and has taken upon himself the role of Prosecutor. In this defence, he addressed the issue of whether he was -- that whether he was a deputy commander of the camp, which was alleged in the amended indictment, instead of the issue whether he was an administrative aide, which is what the Trial Chamber found. According to him, under Article 21 of the Statute, he claims that the Trial Chamber has only to determine whether allegations contained in the indictment are true and they must not exceed the framework of the said indictment by determining possible criminal responsibility of the accused which he has not been charged with. Radic has specifically raised the issue that joint criminal enterprise is not to be found in the indictment and he said specifically that the Trial Chamber impermissibly expanded the form of the indictment by expanding the form of responsibility in said indictment. Kvocka specifically complains that the Prosecution did not specifically allege in the amended indictment that he had become the deputy commander of the police station department. Zigic, particularly, complains about being convicted for offences for which in fact he was not charged. The onus is on the appellants to demonstrate that the Chamber returned convictions on the basis of material facts not pleaded in the amended indictment and that if it is proved that the Trial Chamber did rely on such facts, the trial was rendered unfair. I will now deal with the specific ground in terms of the failure to plead joint criminal enterprise in the indictment, the allegation by the appellants. The first point is that the amended indictment specifically alleged that the accused were responsible for the crimes set out in the amended indictment pursuant to Article 7(1) and 7(3), and in relation to 7(1), that it was intended to incorporate any and all forms of individual criminal responsibility as set forth in Article 7(1). The Tadic appeal judgement was quite pellucid in indicating that Article 7(1) incorporated notions of common purpose and joint criminal enterprise. The appellants were therefore on general notice of the Prosecution's intention to rely upon this form of individual criminal responsibility. And if I may say in passing, reference has been made perennially about the Tadic judgement. Reference has been made perennially from the inception of this case, from the time in fact when the indictment was being queried, with regard to forms of liability as found in Tadic. It does not require any type of esoteric or any type of sophisticated analysis to appreciate that this was a camp case, consistent with in fact those -- with that mandate that in fact Tadic outlined in terms of the three types of possible JCE. So when my friends speak of the fact that they are lawyers, if in fact you are lawyers, it is so easier to interpret based on the factual scenario, apart from in the indictment, that this must have been a case of joint criminal enterprise. But it goes more than that. No one doubts that Article 24 and 21 -- 21, 4, A, delineates the right of an accused to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands, re: the nature and cause of the charge against him. But the indictment does not stand in isolation. It is one part of a process which includes pre-trial procedures of discovery and trial preparation. This is not to say, however, that the Prosecution is allowed a certain licence to do what it wants. It must in fact at the end of the day maintain the regime and the regimen that is expected of any indictment in terms of setting out what is in fact the nature of the charge and the material particulars. However, the Tribunal jurisprudence has been quite emphatic in stating that we cannot appear to impose national, jurisdictional rules and national rules of procedure on this Tribunal. Many an article has been written about the sui generis quality of this trial, an amalgam, as it were, a coslition of jurisprudential learning, so that we cannot expect the same kind of regimen that would one find in a local jurisdiction where crimes are particularised specifically, as opposed to situation dealing with international war crimes more so in a situation like the Omarska camp, which was deemed to be a criminal entity, a criminal enterprise, as it were. This is not to say, as I said before, and this is the proviso. The Prosecution still has the responsibility to delineate the nature of the charge so that in fact the accused person can respond in relevant terms. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief filed in April of 1999 referred to the principle of common criminal purpose or unlawful common enterprise as part of the discussion of 7(1). I wish to remind this learned Tribunal that this case didn't start until 2000, specifically in March of 2000, and was further adjourned to May of 2000 to accommodate Prcac's late entry into the case. So this is a case where, for example, the whole common criminal purpose hovered like the proverbial angel over their heads. And they would have been quite aware of what in fact was being put forward by the Prosecution. Furthermore, it is clear to all of the appellants at the time of the Prosecution's opening statement in February 2000 that the Prosecution was relying on the theory of common purpose based on the three categories in Tadic. None of the appellants objected at that stage to a theory of common purpose or joint criminal enterprise. Nor in fact did any of the appellants raise it in their 98 bis application hearing. In this instance, the appellants alleged lack of responsibility under Article 1, that is in the 98 bis hearing, and the Article 7(3) was fully addressed in the context of the evidence but not in the context of any alleged defect in the indictment. The appellants never indicated at the trial that they were in some way hampered in the conduct of their cross-examination of the particular witnesses. If in fact they made that complaint, it was only in relation to the issue of disclosure which has been appropriately marked out by the various motions filed and responded to. It was not in relation to the form of the indictment. I refer particularly to T646 and 658, the Prosecution opening statement, that confirm this particular position of the Prosecution. Kvocka, although belatedly raised the issue in his final brief is that the Prosecution was trying to expand the responsibility of the accused and the Trial Chamber reasonably noted that the Prosecution should and be limited to prove the counts from the indictment during the case. The Prosecution submits that the amended indictment did not have any type of lacuna. More particularly, that it did not materially impair the ability of the accused to prepare the defence. It is prudent to consider, for example, that there is an evolving law with regard to the form of the indictment. However, there are certain basic tenets which I will succinctly outline. The Prosecution must be accorded a degree of flexibility in drafting indictments. And it is permissible to charge multiple forms of individual responsibility when the Prosecution intends to rely on each of them. The jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal makes it clear, and I refer to the Celebici appeal judgement, if I may quote verbatim, "Although greater specificity in drafting indictment is desirable, failure to identify, expressly the exact mode of participation is not necessarily fatal to an indictment if it nevertheless makes clear to the accused the nature and the cause of the charge against him." The primary question, then, is whether the failure to make express reference to a particular mode of responsibility in the said amended indictment has created the type of ambiguity that has unfairly prejudiced the accused in the preparation of his defence. And this does not in fact take away the discretion of a Trial Chamber to choose the most appropriate form of participation under Article 7(1) of the Statute to describe the responsibility of the accused person. However, the Krnojelac appeals judgement has held that the Prosecution's obligation, and I refer to paragraph 139, to draw up a sufficiently precise indictment must be interpreted in the light of Articles 21(2), 21(4)(a) and 21(4)(b) of the Statute which states that: In the determination of charges against the accused, he shall be entitled to a fair hearing and to be informed of the nature and cause of the charge against him and to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. And specifically in relation to Prcac, this becomes extremely relevant, because one would remember that he came on board pretty late in the day and he was afforded time, and he did not complain. And I intend to refer later on to specific motions and decisions to specific Status Conferences where he acquiesced to the entire process without complaint. Krnojelac appeal judgement confirms that paragraph 131 translate into an obligation on the part of the Prosecution to state the material facts on the pending charges in the indictment but not the evidence by which such facts are to be proved. And we are saying in fact in relation to JCE that that material fact was in fact there in the indictment and they were quite privy and would have had notice to what was required of them. The bottom line is whether an indictment is pleaded with sufficient particularity is dependent on whether it sets out the material facts of the Prosecution's case with enough detail, enough detail, to inform a defendant clearly of the charges. The Kupreskic appeal judgement in paragraph 132 was confirmed that the fundamental rule of thumb as set out in Kupreskic is that the materiality of the particular fact cannot be determined in the abstract. It depends on the objective of the Prosecution's case. A decisive factor in determining the degree of specificity with which the Prosecution is required to particularise the facts of its case is the nature of the alleged criminal conduct of the accused. One would expect, then, that if you have a situation involving a camp case, where you have various sets of crimes being committed, at various times and at various opportunities, if I may so describe it, one cannot expect the same degree of specificity that one would obtain, that one would find in a situation where in fact you're dealing possibly with a case like Vasiljevic, involving one particular incident. No one doubts that the Krnojelac appeal judgement indicates and considers that ambiguity should be avoided and holds that when it arises the Prosecution must identify precisely the form or forms of liability alleged for each count as soon as possible and in any event before the start of the trial. It went on to say, however, that the Appeals Chamber considers that it is preferable for an indictment alleging the accused's responsibility as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to refer to the particular form of joint criminal enterprise envisaged. However, this does not, in principle, prevent the Prosecution from pleading elsewhere than in the indictment. For instance, in a pre-trial brief, the legal theory which it believes best demonstrates that the crime or crimes alleged are imputable to the accused in law in the light of the facts alleged. The option, however, is limited by the need to guarantee the accused a fair trial. Specifically, the amended indictment contained all of the requisite allegations to warn the appellants of the crimes of which they were charged. It set out the factual basis for these charges, including the times, the places, and the nature of the offences. And despite the absence of an express reference to the concept of joint criminal enterprise, the amended indictment in this case set out the basic parameters of the Prosecution's case in this regard. It referred to the unlawful segregation, detention and confinement of non-Serbs in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps, the terrible conditions inflicted upon the detainees. It stated as part of the broader goal of permanently removing non-Serb inhabitants of the territory forming part of the planned Bosnian Serb state. It contained the general time frames of the commission of offences.

Yes, of course in fact many times in fact, you know, there can be incidents of selective compassion. But does that in fact eradicate liability in a JCE, in a systemic JCE as what obtains in this present situation? I dare say no. The Court in fact made firm findings that he was resolutely efficient, that if in fact there were problems in the list he would solve these problems. If in fact people ace names were missing he would solve these problems. He would, for example, in the case of Smail Duratovic, Mujo wanted him to be moved from the "white house" to his room. This was done with the permission with the guards who consulted with Prcac. So there is in fact stark evidence of a relationship between movements within the camp and one must remember the very stark reality that witnesses said once you entered "white house," you -- in fact very few people left there alive. There was the "white house," there was the "red house." There was the interrogation room. Where was Prcac's office? On the same corridor. Yet in fact in his interview he says in fact "I only saw two bodies." Yet there was a witness who came on the 23rd of July who said in fact that there were some nine bodies in the camp spread out for the last week and Prcac had in fact been there about a week and a half. So that in fact not only did he have knowledge but that knowledge was subsumed and became intent because the bottom line is in fact, for example, he was doing particular things to assist the systemic criminal enterprise. I mean, Your Honours, as I said before, it may well be in fact because of economy I would not be able to go into it in detail, but I think our brief basically maps out the role of these lists, the role of Prcac in the JCE. And we stand by these arguments. In relation to the question of the credibility of the witnesses, my friend has made again heavy weather of certain witnesses. Again, we have addressed this, especially Mesan Omer. He speaks about the issue of identification. What is the relevance of identification? You're talking about an incident that took place on the 6th of August, where Prcac is with the list. And some 50 people go into a bus and they just disappear. And you're saying for example that Mesan Omer couldn't identify him in court. And we all know what the law is with regard in Court and identification. And we have the authority of Furundzija, which states Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very categorically that sometimes a particular individual in those camp scenarios may have some peculiar, idiosyncratic feature. And what was his feature? The list. He was the man handling the list. He was the man moving around. And this particular witness gave a very good physical description of him at that point in time. More importantly, the identification, or I should say the reliability of that identification, is further confirmed by other witnesses who supported this particular witness on material particulars as they relate to identification. So to the extent, for example, you're saying, then -- apart from that, you have the very admission of the appellant saying that he was there on that day. So what is the problem with identification? And we are not saying, for example, that he was the only man with a list. Because on that particular day there were at least two individuals. The bottom line is that he is part of a JCE, you know. And there was a particular structure in place. And there were particular modus operandi taking place by Prcac, that affects the efficient running of the camp. Again I wish to adopt our arguments in relation to Omer Mesan. And I think in fact, if I may say so without raising a flag, basically we have in fact mapped out our responses in relation to the credibility of witnesses in terms of inconsistencies and how they are to be addressed by the Court. And I dare say in fact my friend runs very close to the road of seeking a re-evaluation because, as Kunarac Appeals Chamber has said, an appeal hearing is not an attempt on the part of counsel to superimpose his view of the facts on the Appeals Chamber. You have to show the relationship between your submissions and an error of fact resulting in a miscarriage of justice. You have to show some kind of fundamental, erroneous fact that took place. I dare say in his submissions in fact my learned friend has not been able to do this. Your Honours, in fact, if I may, I think, as I said before, on the whole issue with regard to disclosure -- oh, yes. I just wish to refer the Court to some documents that not only indicate in fact that JCE was on board from the inception, but also in the context of disclosure exercised, because in fact I do recall one particular motion where in fact Prcac was invited to cross-examine witnesses and he simply refused. There was no motion and the case went on and the witnesses weren't cross-examined. But the bottom line is and I think it's imperative that I establish this particular point. When you look at the Status Conferences that dealt with the issue of these witnesses, that dealt with the issue of the ten witnesses that they are saying for example were new witnesses, that they were not new witnesses, that the Court requested of them whether in fact they needed adjournments. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. The sitting is resumed. Thank you. Who will speak now for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This afternoon, I'll be addressing you mainly on -- responding to the appellant Radic's appeal, but in doing so I'll also be speaking to you this afternoon about some common grounds of appeal, and in fact, the first ground of appeal that I'll begin this afternoon's submissions with is Radic's ground 1B concerning the confidential schedules as it related to the Trial Chamber's reasoned opinion. It's a common ground of appeal raised not just by Radic but also by Kvocka and Zigic especially. The question is this: Did the Trial Chamber err by not setting out in its judgement separate factual findings on each and every one of the hundreds of incidents listed in the schedules A through E? In reality, the question really boils down to this: Did the Trial Chamber render a proper, reasoned decision? My friend, my colleague, Mr. Carmona, has already addressed you this morning on the issues relating to fair notice of charges in the indictment. But this is something different. This is about whether the Trial Chamber rendered a reasoned opinion. And in our view, the only answer to this is yes. The Trial Chamber set out its material findings of fact, the evidence on which those findings were based, and the reasons why, in law, those facts rendered the accused criminally liable for the crimes based on the case, based on the evidence before it. This Appeals Chamber has stressed that the extent of the duty to provide a reasoned opinion will obviously vary depending on the circumstances of the case and the nature of the decision involved. In our submission, in a case of this nature, calling for an assessment of the criminal liability of various participants in a system of ill-treatment - that is, JCE category 2 as it's known in this Tribunal - involving crimes being committed on a daily basis, many crimes being committed simultaneously, some crimes being committed continuously, against thousands of victims detained there, thousands of people detained there for a period of three months, it would be near impossible to make factual findings on every single incident. But more importantly, in our submission, nor is it necessary to do so. The Trial Chamber's approach of analysing the overwhelming evidence of killings, of beatings, of physical and mental violence, sexual violence, the degrading conditions of detention, as exemplified by the incidents in the confidential schedules, to find beyond reasonable doubt that it supported a system of ill-treatment to persecute through these, what we could call core acts, and then examining and again finding beyond reasonable doubt each accused's material and mental contributions, that that was an appropriate framework in this context of a joint criminal enterprise category 2, in which to assess their liability. If we look at the judgement, in parts 2 and parts 4, the Trial Chamber has in fact referred to a vast proportion of the incidents or the victims, let's say, in the schedules: the beatings, the murders, the tortures, the rapes, the sexual violence, the inhumane conditions. And on the basis of this evidence, it found beyond reasonable doubt that this persecutory system of ill-treatment existed and was conducted on discriminatory grounds. From this evidence, it was able to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that various crimes were committed within this persecutory system of ill-treatment, with an intensity, a frequency, a regularity, indeed a systematicity, so as to be encompassed in the persecutory system of ill-treatment. And we see then in part 4 again the Trial Chamber refers to a very large proportion of the incidents in the schedules when it comes to focus on the individual contributions, the individual involvement, and the mens rea of each accused. Is there an inconsistency between the level of detail given in the schedules but then the Trial Chamber not, as it were, following through in terms of making findings on each and every single item, as Mr. Fila suggested? In our submission, no. Schedules like this can serve a variety of purposes. It can be put forward for a number of reasons. And here, the reason it was put forward, the reason why the schedules came into existence, as it were, were to give the accused more precision. It was a fairness issue. To tell them about the case against them. This doesn't transform them into somehow becoming the indictment or the material facts of the indictment. If we look at the decision on the form of the indictment which was handed down, delivered on the 12th of April, 1994, the Prosecution was ordered to give particulars to the indictment and was ordered to identify, insofar as it could, the names of the victims of the crimes which occurred in Omarska and details and rough dates on when they occurred. The Prosecution, accordingly, filed an amended indictment and the schedules, and this was only fair. If we look at a statement in the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber decision, of course it was rendered afterwards, but the principle still remains the same, at paragraph 117: "An accused must know whether the system he is charged with having contributed to involves all the acts being prosecuted or only some of them." But the Prosecution's case, liability, was never limited to the named victims, the named, individualised, itemised incidents. We need only look at the first line of each schedule, which refers to all prisoners confined in Omarska camp during the period, or, for example, all prisoners killed in Omarska camp in the period, before going on to list specific incidents. In our submission, the single itemised incidents listed in the schedules were always only illustrative of a larger pool of crimes for which the accused were to be held liable because they formed part of the system of ill-treatment. What was clear is that the accused were being charged and ultimately held liable on the basis of a system of crimes, comprised of acts to maltreat and subjugate the non-Serb detainees on a discriminatory basis, including murder, torture, beatings, detention, and inhumane conditions and sexual violence - most importantly, for what they did, knowingly and intentionally, to further that system. The only limitation placed on this liability was the one that was placed by the 98 bis decision, the half time decision, which held that each accused would only be responsible for the crimes during the temporal post of his time, and I won't say any more on that. I think my colleagues Ms. Rashid and Mr. Carmona have addressed you quite clearly on our position on that. Many cases in this Tribunal have used similar approaches. For example, we see in cases like Stakic and Tuta Stela. The Trial Chamber there didn't set out in its opinion each and every episode of persecution that occurred, but rather that the persecution was found based on sufficient proof of evidence of some incidents of persecutory acts. It's even akin, and I'm not suggesting it was done in the same way, but it is even drawing somewhat closely to the representative-sample approach that we have seen in cases like Galic. In that case, in Galic, the Trial Chamber said there that the schedules served a procedural requirement of proper notice but should not be understood as reducing the Prosecution's case to the scheduled incidents. We suggest that what the Trial Chamber has done here is very similar in some ways to what was done in Galic, where the Trial Chamber saw the scheduled incidents as exemplifying an overall situation, and a wider campaign; in that case, in Sarajevo. And just as here, in the Galic case as well, much evidence was led tending to support the Prosecution's general case which indeed went beyond the scheduled incidents. The final point that I'll make on this ground is that there have been World War II camp cases, such as the Belsen trial and the Dachau trial which show as well evidence being led on a number of single episodes to represent the larger picture of the systematic criminal conduct. In summary, our submission is that the Trial Chamber's reasoned opinion suffers no defect in not having itemised each incident in the schedule, but rather treating the incidents as evidence from which to find beyond reasonable doubt as to the nature of the system, its components, and what each accused's role was in it. I'll turn now to the area upon which Mr. Fila finished his submissions on Tuesday, and now I turn more specifically to grounds raised by the appellant Mr. Radic. And in particular, I'll turn now to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. his convictions for persecution and torture, based on rape and sexual violence. And I'd like to spend a little bit of time on this area, not only because of the obvious importance that Mr. Fila and his client have placed on them. I think Mr. Fila referred to it as the essential point for Radic. But also because of the importance the Trial Chamber placed on his acts of rape and sexual violence, to find that he contributed significantly to furthering the criminal goals of this camp. The Trial Chamber saw these criminal actions by Radic as one of the key ways -- by no means the only way, but indeed one of the key ways in which Radic contributed to this joint criminal enterprise to persecute and maltreat non-Serbs in Omarska camp. And to begin with, I have to say that I was struck by Mr. Fila's comment when he began the other day and he said, and I quote from him: "In a war, people fight, but people do not rape in a war." Regrettably, people do rape in such a context. And that's exactly why -- well, it's one of the reasons why Mr. Radic is here before you today. That's what he has been convicted of. Turning first to the rape of Witness K. The appellant's submissions really amount to nothing more than his view about why Witness K was not credible, and in his opinion, he said she conjured it all up. His arguments have simply repeated his trial arguments rather than meeting the appellate standard of review of errors of fact and showing that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have done so. But before I come to his direct arguments, I would like to speak about two sets of submissions that Mr. Fila made on Tuesday about Witness K, which in our opinion were quite improper and, in fact, I have to ask Your Honours to exclude those from your consideration. In order to do this, I need to go into private session for a couple of minutes. I don't want to compound the problem that arose the other day, the confidentiality issue that may have occurred on Tuesday. So I've foreshadowed this with Madam Registrar and what I say next, in the next few minutes, should remain within private session.
