utterances.text: Any objection? Then it is so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, there was no unreasonableness in the Trial Chamber having accepted Witness K as a credible witness, notwithstanding some inconsistencies and contradictions in her evidence. Mr. Fila mentioned some of these the other day, some discrepancies between the 1995 statement and her trial testimony, her failure to mention this rape to a journalist in 1993, and her failure to mention to the Prosecutor in 1995 that she had earlier spoken to a journalist. Our response brief has counted each point, so I don't need to go back into that. But just to give by way of an example as to why it was not unreasonable, in terms of not mentioning the incident to the journalist in 1993, in our submission, the appellant has not shown that it was unreasonable, in light of the sexual and intensely personal nature of the crime, for the Trial Chamber to have deemed irrelevant her failure to mention her rape by Radic to the journalist then, even if she had told the journalist about being raped by Sikirica somewhere else. I should also point out that this witness was thoroughly cross-examined about this issue, and in fact Judge Wald had asked her directly: Why did you feel you could talk about this very terrible experience in Keraterm and not about an equally bad experience in Omarska? So no unreasonableness arises by the Trial Chamber being alive to this discrepancy, adjudging her as credible. The appellant also argued strenuously that the Trial Chamber didn't address all the discrepancies between her statement and her trial testimony, and his submissions were that the two accounts were very, very different, very divergent. He said it happened like this, it happened like that. I invite Your Honours to look at these. You'll see the differences. They are relatively inconsequential. But secondly, any discrepancies were explored in cross-examination and canvassed in his final trial brief, and there's no indication, if one looks at the Trial Chamber's judgement that they did not properly take them into account. I'd like to turn to a slightly different point that he made on Tuesday in his brief when he referred to certain findings being made by the Sikirica Trial Chamber about this witness. And if I understand him correctly, what he seems to be asking Your Honours, this Bench, is to take note of the Sikirica Trial Chamber's findings on Witness K. The only way, putting aside matters of common knowledge, the only way that a Chamber, one Chamber, can take judicial notice of another Trial Chamber's factual findings is through Rule 94(B) on adjudicated facts. Now, it would be a first, I believe, for this Chamber for you to actually use this Rule in this way, but theoretically it could be possible for you to do so. We don't -- we're not going to explore that question today, but what we are -- what our submission is that even if theoretically you could do so, it's not possible to do so here because the requirements of Rule 94(B) can't be met. For a fact to be capable of admission under this Rule, it has to have been truly adjudicated. It can't have been based on a plea agreement in previous cases. And here, the finding that Mr. Radic has asked you to notice, or note, comes from a plea agreement, and like all plea agreements, its facts are not the outcome of litigation but the consensus of parties. I think it's also worth noting that the Sikirica Trial Chamber didn't actually acquit Sikirica of raping K in its 98 bis decision, the September decision, and in its sentencing decision it made no determination on the credibility of this witness. So there's no basis for saying, as Mr. Fila did, that we can see clearly in Keraterm Trial Chamber that nobody believed her, neither the Prosecution nor the Trial Chamber. Indeed, we would query, the Prosecution would query whether a Trial Chamber's assessment in one trial about a witness's credibility could ever conceivably be judicially noticed by another Trial Chamber as an adjudicated fact. Why is this? A Trial Chamber can rely on a witness's testimony on one matter, but not on another, unless, of course, the reason enures to some inherent problem with the witness's credibility, so as to affect the witness's credit on all his or her evidence. And we see, for example, this being mentioned by the Celebici Appeals Chamber in paragraph 479. If we apply this logic, then even if another Trial Chamber, the Sikirica Trial Chamber, or even indeed if this Trial Chamber had not been prepared to rely on her evidence that she was raped by Sikirica in Keraterm, this wouldn't bear upon the Trial Chamber's acceptance of her evidence about being raped by another person, Radic, somewhere else, in Omarska. And we saw this very clearly in the Kunarac Trial Chamber's decision, where certain witnesses, I note in particular FWS 87 and 95, where the Trial Chamber was prepared to accept a rape victim's evidence for some rapes but not for others. The final point I make on this is that it's clear that the Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber, was fully alive to Witness K's evidence that she had given in that Sikirica trial, because in June of 2001, she was brought back for cross-examination before this Trial Chamber, and she was directly asked about the inconsistencies in her account about that rape, which had arisen during her Sikirica trial evidence. So this Trial Chamber, when I say this one, the Kvocka and others Trial Chamber, therefore would have been privy to see some of the differences between Witness K's evidence about being raped by Radic and being raped by Sikirica in Keraterm, and I just note one particular difference and that is an identification difference. She knew in terms of recognised Radic. She had seen him around before the incident had occurred at Omarska, whereas with Sikirica, she only saw him that morning for the first time. In summary, Your Honours, our submission is that this Appeals Chamber should not take judicial notice of any finding by the Sikirica Trial Chamber about this witness, and you actually must exclude it from your consideration. I turn now to deal with the sexual violence on Witness J. Mr. Fila was very brief the other day on this, and so I'll accordingly also be very brief. No error arises in the Trial Chamber having found that he sexually assaulted Witness J. Basically what he's done is re-argued his trial position, which the Trial Chamber addressed, that it was -- I think, to be best explained, his argument is best explained by the word -- he says that it was a coincidence that Witness J was sexually assaulted by the man called Kapitan in a similar way. And simply by putting this forward yet again, it does not establish error of fact. I'll turn to his more generic argument that he made about the sexual violence upon Witness J and Witness F, Sifeta Susic and Zlata Cikota. He has made a generic argument to the effect that his conduct against witness J and F and Susic and Cikota was not serious enough, or sufficiently grave to amount to serious violations of international humanitarian law within the Tribunal's jurisdiction. I must confess to not having fully followed or understood properly his argument at the beginning of his submissions about Article 2 of the Statute, because, of course, the accused were not convicted under Article 2 but under Articles 3 and 5. And the concept of gravity of the crime for persecution and torture is not tied to any question of what crimes can be considered to be grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions under Article 2. So I'll leave that to one side. The most important point is that I think that he's significantly downplayed the seriousness of this conduct, and I think we need to bring it back into perspective by looking at the criminal conduct. For Witness F, Radic took her into a room, into the room, and he said he could help her if she slept with him and then, to quote her evidence, he touched her female parts. For Sifeta Susic, Radic grabbed her as she was clearing away a table and put her on his knee, saying: It's better for me to rape you than someone else. For Zlata Cikota, one day -- I believe it was in his office, I may not have got that part of the evidence quite in my mind, but one day he had an encounter with her and he grabbed her breasts, and when she said, "I'm just an old woman," he replied, "Well, you're good, it doesn't really matter." And finally for Witness J, and of this group I think one would agree this was the most serious of the conducts, he pushed her roughly against a wall, he pushed up her clothes, he touched her breasts and genitals, and then after unsuccessfully trying to effect sexual penetration, he ejaculated on her leg. In effect, Radic by his submissions is contending that this sexual bullying, these threats to rape, these sexual touchings and these sexual assaults on these women held in captivity, in this overwhelmingly threatening environment, by him, who to them was a person in authority let's not forget, he's saying that they're not serious enough for torture and persecution or not serious enough to be grave violations of international humanitarian law. We know that torture for both Article 3 and Article 5 must cause the victim severe pain and suffering. We also know the gravity of harm has both objective and subjective components. Here it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have found that the pain and suffering inflicted upon the victims was severe. Just to look at the words of Sifeta Susic. She said: "I felt terrible, dreadful. I can't describe it in words." Given the victim's extraordinary vulnerability, their imprisonment in a place where violence against detainees was the rule, not the exception, their knowledge of Radic's position that he could roam around the camp at will and order their presence before them, their knowledge or suspicion that other women were being raped or otherwise sexually assaulted in the camp, and therefore, the threat was very real that they could be subjected to sexual violence at Radic's whim. With this in mind, it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have assessed the gravity as sufficient for torture, and that's why it's criminalised here. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If Your Honours did take the view that the gravity did not meet the sufficiency of gravity for harm for torture at the very least, Your Honours, this conduct amounts to outrages upon personal dignity, at least for the threat-type comments, and I would point Your Honours to cases or examples of incidents of sexual assaults of a similarly we might call it non-penetrative nature; Kunarac, which was naked dancing; Furundzija, which was a girl being forced to stand naked before a group of men; and Tadic, in a male context, by forcing one person to lick the naked bottom of another person. Those were held sufficient to amount to sexual assault, and outrages against personal dignity. Likewise, when we think about persecution, under Article 5, of course, this can -- persecution can require either that the act be an enumerated crime or entail the denial of other fundamental human rights, provided that separately or cumulatively the acts are of the same gravity or severity as the other enumerated crimes in Article 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to the interpreters. Again, when we see Radic's conduct not in isolation but cumulatively, with all the other persecutory acts that these women endured in Omarska, the Trial Chamber made no error in finding that the women were persecuted by these acts. And again, I make the caveat that at the minimum, I guess you would say, the acts rise to the level of being inhumane acts and therefore to be able to be absorbed into the wider crime of persecution. The final area that I'll turn to in this group of the rape and sexual violence crimes was the appellant's arguments concerning the Trial Chamber's use of the evidence that he had raped Witness AT as Rule 93 evidence. The legal submissions I make will also be common for the appellant Zigic's arguments. The facts differ because the nature of the evidence differs, but the legal submissions I make are the same. In our submission, the Trial Chamber made no error by taking into account Radic's rape of AT, Witness AT, as evidence of a consist pattern of conduct under Rule 93, in consideration of his charged crimes of rape and sexual violence. And we recall that Witness AT attested that at first Radic helped her, he gave her some food, he moved her husband into the "glass house"; but one night he took her to the conference room with the sponge mattress on the floor, he told her to undress and he forced her to have sexual intercourse. The evidence is that he raped Witness AT is clearly relevant and probative, and in our submission it's not outweighed by its prejudicial value. So we're right within the parameters of the Appeal Chamber's decision in Bagosora on the 19th of December, 2003. What we say is that it was very probative evidence of his what we would call modus operandi, his quid pro quo system of asking women to have sex with him in exchange for assistance, and then, upon their refusal, sexually assaulting them. As such, the Trial Chamber was not in error to use this evidence to corroborate Witness K and J. I don't say for one moment that K and J did need corroboration; their evidence stands as enough to be sufficient to prove the crimes that occurred against them. But basically, Witness AT's evidence is further corroboration for their evidence. And if we look at other cases in the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise again. Many cases have used Rule 93. I note the Strugar decision, Trial Chamber's decision on the 22nd of January, 2004 and Kupreskic Appeals Chamber decision at 321. I also note that in the Kunarac case for the accused Vukovic, there the Trial Chamber used evidence of uncharged oral rape on Witness 51 as evidence in proof of the charged rape. And we see from these cases that this evidence under Rule 93 is often used for this purpose of corroborating other evidence. Here, Radic used the same quid pro quo system when he raped K and assaulted J. Before sexually assaulting J, he told her, while she was in the serious category of detainees, but he knew an inspector, and in return for his assistance, he'd ask for, in Witness J's words, a counter-service. For Witness K, Radic initially tried to coerce her into having sex with him by saying that if she agreed, her children would not be killed. That's the evidence of those victims. We reject his submissions that he made that this evidence - this evidence - must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. What has to be proved beyond reasonable doubt are the charged crimes, the rape of K, the sexual assault on Witness J. The Krnojelac Trial Chamber noted that Rule 93 evidence is similar to circumstantial evidence. Just as each piece of evidence in a circumstantial case doesn't need to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, neither does evidence under Rule 93. It's the ultimate fact which must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, not each piece of evidence that goes towards proof of that. And the closest analogy that we can see from national systems would be in the common law use of similar-fact evidence, and similar-fact evidence of strikingly similar evidence, once admitted into court, is treated as one further piece of evidence for the fact-finder to consider in its overall assessment of the evidence in the case. Besides this, there is no indication, in fact, when you look at the judgement, that the Trial Chamber's evaluation of Witness AT's evidence differed from any other way and that they applied some different standard that they applied to the examination of the other witnesses. So the point is possibly even moot. The final point I'll make just concerns his notice or fairness arguments. And Mr. Fila the other day described Witness AT's evidence as like a stone dropping from the sky. And I must say, I like the expression, it's very evocative; but I have to disagree with its use in this context. The Defence received a proffer of this witness's testimony, the proffer of 14 September 2000, before she testified in October 2000, thereby complying with its obligations under 66(A), and most importantly raised no objection when the evidence was led. Out of fairness to the accused, the rape wasn't added to the indictment, but this doesn't mean the Trial Chamber should be precluded from using it as evidence of the charged crimes, especially in view of his waiver. The Prosecution understands that Rule 65 ter may now well require a Prosecutor -- the Prosecution to set out in a pre-trial brief each count in the evidence, but the Rule entered into force on the 4th of May, 2001, whereas this disclosure was done in October of 2000. And when confronted by a similar issue - identical issue, in fact - in the Kupreskic case, this Chamber didn't hold the Prosecution to the more exacting disclosure obligations unless the interests of justice so compelled. And we submit that in that case, the interests of justice did not so compel the higher standard and therefore, our submission is that he was fully on notice in an appropriate way. In summary, Your Honours, our submission is that Radic's grounds on his crimes of rape and sexual violence must all be dismissed. I'll turn now to look more at his grounds in ground 4 A through C about the findings on his position and duties, the crimes committed by the guards on his shift, and his knowledge of the general camp conditions and abusive treatment. And again, he was brief the other day. Of course, his Appeal Brief is before you. And in the same way, our response brief, which has gone through this in some detail, is before you and I won't be long today on these points. But I think what comes out very clearly is that the appellant Radic is really only proposing his preferred alternative assessment of the evidence, rather than showing the apellable error. On the first issue about his position as guard shift leader, there was no error in the Trial Chamber having found that Radic was a guard shift leader who had and who exercised substantial authority over guards in his shift and that he used his power to prevent crimes selectively, while ignoring the vast majority. This is especially so in light of the overwhelming witnesses' testimony about what they saw, what they heard, and what they experienced Mr. Radic do and what Mr. Radic told them himself. Just to name some examples, he was present when new detainees arrived, he would register them, he was present during guard shift change-overs, and he gave assignments to guards, according to Witness J's evidence. They'd report to him when he took up duty for their shift. He walked around the camp with them and he would sit in the duty room with the other shift leaders and deputy commander and commander, whoever was on the shift. Nor in our submission was it an error for the Trial Chamber to have inferred from his selective assistance and his selective protection, such as I've already described in relation to the women detainees or to certain of his old friends from home, that he was able to do so because he had some degree of power or authority in the camp. And there's no way the Trial Chamber's findings could be possibly interpreted or boiled down to being based on people simply calling it Krkan's shift because they knew him from before the war. I want to spend a little bit more time on a question that he called the most important for his appeal or one of the most important and that is the Trial Chamber's finding that he did not have Article 7(3) liability and hence he could not have had sufficient authority over guards for his Article 7(1) liability in a JCE. And this ties in to the question that His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen posed the other day. Not only is the appellant actually misstating the Trial Chamber's findings on Radic's Article 7(3) liability but he's confusing two very different modes of liability. The first point: The Trial Chamber did not actually in fact make definitive findings on whether Radic had effective control over the guards in terms of the superior-subordinate relationship that's needed for 7(3) liability. In fact, if you look at paragraph 570, the Trial Chamber expressly declined to rule on this, since his liability for the crimes was already covered. But even if the Trial Chamber had found that Radic had no effective control over the guards for 7(3) - and we do see that there is a certain ambivalence in paragraph 570 - this would not be inconsistent with the finding that he was a guard shift leader who exercised significant authority and power over the guards. A person can exercise significant authority over others without being necessarily their superior for the purposes of 7(3). And nor is liability under 7(1), as a co-perpetrator of a JCE dependent upon a finding of superiority in the sense of 7(3). Turning to the Trial Chamber's findings about the crimes committed on the -- by the guards on Radic's shift, and in particular, the finding that the guards on his shift committed numerous serious and brutal crimes, and as his -- as their shift leader, he never exercised any authority to stop them, and this sort of air of permissiveness, this tolerance, further encouraged their continuance. Witnesses were pretty much all united on one thing, that this shift, Radic's shift, was the worst of the three. You had guards like Predojevic, Popovic, Paspalj, Zivko Marmat, a character by the name of the karate kid, and outsiders who came in, Knezevic and Tadic and Zigic, who came in to do their deeds. In fact, as found by the Trial Chamber, some of the most memorable beatings happened on this shift, such as Zigic's beating of Kapetanovic and Kiki. And another memorable beating done by guards on Radic's shift, the murder of Rizah Hadzalic on the pista. Radic seems to say: I couldn't stop these guys. No one listened to my orders. It was absolute mayhem. So how could I be responsible? The first thing is that the evidence doesn't actually point -- doesn't actually bear that particular line out. He did stop some crimes and prevent others. In fact, in evidence, he said so himself. He gave an example of where he'd stopped and spoken to a guard in the restaurant who had been beating somebody. He also referred to allowing Witness J to have -- receive a visitor who would bring her food and the like. But the more important point is that to say that he should not be responsible for their crimes actually misunderstands the basis for his liability. His liability is not under 7(3) for failing to prevent or failing to pressure the crimes of these guards. Sure, his failure to exercise authority to stop the guards did form part of his contribution to the system by tacitly encouraging and condoning the guards' behaviour and generally adding to this air of permissiveness, but his liability is in fact based on his contribution to furthering this system of ill-treatment, knowingly and intentionally. Finally, turning to the appellant's argument that the Trial Chamber erred in rejecting his claim that he didn't see or hear or notice evidence of abuses in the entire three months, and rather, finding that he was, in his position, exposed on a daily basis to killings and tortures and other abuses. Your Honours, we'd ask what other conclusion could have been drawn. The horrors on the pista were seen by all, but not by him, even though he was standing often, on his own words, at the glass circular window in the administration building, looking out. Dead bodies could be seen by all, or many in the camp on a daily basis, but not by him, despite walking around and freely roaming around for three months? Screams and cries and groans and moans could be heard coming from the interrogation room by people in the restaurant, the floor below. And although Radic was in the room next door, he heard only "the sound of furniture falling." Even the typist in that room, DD/10, agreed you could hear the abuses. The women detainees often saw blood and beating instruments in the interrogation rooms, but he never did? He never saw the beatings of new detainees upon arrival when they were made to run through a gauntlet of people beating them? And although he frequently took detainees to the interrogations and then would a accompany them back, he only noticed, on his words, some sort of long faces and red eyes? Not to mention his own participation in the crimes. No other reasonable conclusion could have been drawn. The final area that I'll address you on concerns the Trial Chamber's findings that Radic was responsible as a co-perpetrator in the joint criminal enterprise. And on Tuesday, Mr. Fila said he couldn't see anything in the judgement which explained why Radic is a co-perpetrator of this JCE. In our submission, to accept his argument that Radic's contribution is not enough and would make a cook or a janitor or some person like this liable actually would ignore all the findings made by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 506 to 561. These were the core factors which enabled the Trial Chamber to reasonably conclude that Radic knew of the criminal system, shared its criminal goals, and participated significantly in it. I can't summarise an entire judgement, obviously, but I guess if I was going to put it into a nutshell, his position as guard shift leader, his authority over other guards; his direct knowledge of abuses in the camp, what he did, and what he didn't do; his personal involvement in rape and sexual violence; these are his contributions which make him liable as a co-perpetrator in the systemic joint criminal enterprise to persecute the non-Serb detainees in the camp through inhumane conditions, murder, torture, beatings and rape. And I invite Your Honours to look at a better summary than I've just tried to do in paragraphs 566 and 571. Regarding his mens rea, I think it's also important to note that the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber highlighted that in the case of a joint criminal enterprise, it's less important to prove that there was this more or less formal agreement between all the participants than to approve their involvement in the system, and in particular, in paragraph 97, the Krnojelac appeals judgement, of course, which you're familiar with, it said: "Since the Trial Chamber's finding showed that the system in place in KP Dom sought to subject non-Serb detainees to inhumane living conditions and ill-treatment on discriminatory grounds, the Trial Chamber should have examined whether or not Krnojelac knew of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the system and agreed to it, without it being necessary to establish that he had entered into an agreement with the guards and soldiers - the principal perpetrators of the crimes committed under the system - to commit those crimes." In other words, in that case, in Krnojelac, the Appeals Chamber has acknowledged that the determination of his intent is based on an accused's knowledge of the system and the fact that he agreed to it. And this is exactly the case we have here for Radic. He would have to show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that he shared the intent. And if we apply the criteria most aptly summarised in Krnojelac Appeals Chamber paragraph 111, if you look at the duties, the time committed, the time over which they were exercised, the knowledge of the system in place, the crimes committed therein, and the discriminatory nature, that same conclusion must be the only one for Mr. Radic, both that he shared the intent to further the system and shared its persecutory goal. So in summary, in our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find him liable for the crimes committed in the camp during its existence as a co-perpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute, kill, murder, torture, detain in inhumane conditions and generally mistreat non-Serbs. When the facts establish that he personally knew of the system of ill-treatment in the camp and he intended to further that criminal enterprise and contributed significantly in that JCE to persecute and abuse the non-Serbs detained in the camp by furthering the system of ill-treatment. Finally, what I'd like to do is just to turn to some of the specific arguments that he raised. And I'd like to try and think of them in term of colloquial arguments and to group them into I think five or six different categories. The first argument he seems to make in terms of why he shouldn't be a co-perpetrator to this JCE is, he says, "Without the sexual-violence crimes, the only finding left is that I stayed." Your Honours, this is a gross simplification, obviously, of the Trial Chamber's findings. But besides, why would we leave out this integral part of his participation? This was one of the key factors that the Trial Chamber looked at. This was how he directly contributed to the system, by committing further egregious acts. The second argument he seems to make is "I tried to leave Omarska. I had no choice to stay. It was my job." In our submission, when his weak protest that he made to Drljaca is seen against his other testimony that there were no repercussions for guards who didn't turn up for work and his own evidence as to never having missed a shift, the Trial Chamber cannot have been unreasonable to reject his argument but that he had no option but to stay in the camp, and in fact, on the overwhelming evidence, to find, as it did at 565, paragraph 565, that he didn't remain in his post reluctantly. And in fact, the camp provided a forum and a power in which to commit the abuses, and by every indication, he participated in crimes without hesitation. The third argument or line of argument that I read in his submissions is to the effect that "well, I was obedient, I had a conformist personality. I was sent to Omarska as my workplace by my superiors and I didn't confront them because I feared for my family." There's a lot of different issues that that concept raises in one package. I'm not clear whether the argument Mr. Fila made about Article 7(4) the other day at the very beginning of his submissions related to this, but to the Prosecution, Article 7(4) clearly states that superior orders are not a defence. But more importantly, neither superior orders or duress are borne out by the evidence. Far from being a reluctant or a sort of begrudging worker who carried out his job, the evidence actually showed that the camp provided that -- the very place for him to commit further abuses. As for the fears that he held for his family, Mr. Fila mentioned in his submissions that Radic had raised the spectre of threats, that his sons would be sent to the army and then killed, the evidence was not quite that direct. And I turn your attention to transcript of the 6th of March transcript of Radic's testimony, page 1069 to 1070. And he said, in answer to a question by Mr. Fila: And I know that if I had surrendered, that it would probably have been to the detriment of my family. And Mr. Fila asked him: Why didn't you run away? Why didn't you throw away your uniform and simply flee? And he said: But, Mr. Fila, I would be signing a death sentence for my family had I done such a thing. I haven't been able to see from his evidence or the interview evidence of some exact, some threat that he's mentioned in submissions about how his sons would be sent to the army and killed. And in any event, in his own words during the trial, he agreed very carefully, very firmly, with a submission put to him, a question by the Prosecution, that no one who left the camp was -- I think the words in the trial -- the evidence at trial was were no one who left the camp was swallowed up by the darkness. The next argument, or the next line that he seems to raise is -- I neither establish the camp nor did I initially know of its nature. I wasn't an essential person. And look, when I took up the post, I wasn't aware that the camp would be like this. My colleague Ms. Rashid's submissions this morning have very much dealt with this. But a co-perpetrator in this sort of systemic JCE doesn't need to know every single last detail of the system, nor every single individual crime committed in it. Once he agrees and he commits to the system, he's responsible for the crimes falling within it. He doesn't need to be a planner, nor in fact does he even need to be essential. Besides, how long would it have taken to get the full picture of what was going on there? I think the Trial Chamber put this very succinctly in paragraph 324 by saying: Evidence of abuses could be seen, heard, and smelled. The three months that he was there must have made it plainly apparent what was going on, and yet he assiduously attended to the camp's functioning and making sure it was running, to the extent that it was his position to do so, in an efficient way. And he basically looked the other way, except when it suited him to offer assistance, not to mention using it as a forum for his own crimes. And it's been mentioned in the briefs, and I believe the other day, that, well, when Radic got there he said: Look, this affair will all be over in two to three days. Well, it wasn't, and he stayed for three months, and he came back shift after shift in that three months. The final argument or line of argument that I can discern in his submission is to the effect that: Well, even if I'd known of some of these abuses, how could I be responsible when I couldn't change the conditions or influence the commission or non-commission of the crimes by these guards, let alone the interrogators? And even if I had protested, the guards would have kept committing their crimes. Firstly, as I've said, this is factually quite incorrect, because he did actually change conditions and he did protect people on a selective basis. And actually, there's evidence on the record that some guards were able to prevent certain bad things happening in the camp during its existence. But most importantly, the line of defence, this line of defence ignores that he actively furthered the camp's awful conditions, in the face of this knowledge. So even if he couldn't stop some crimes or he had no material ability to prevent some, or some guards were truly these unstoppable forces, which seems apparent that some of these people were indeed these sort of wild forces that couldn't be stopped, his liability stems from his knowingly and intentionally making significant contributions in the face of all that knowledge, doing his bit to this system of mistreatment. He never missed a shift, not once in three months. In conclusion, Your Honours, the appellant cannot show and has not shown that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to have found that Radic, through his material and mental contributions to the joint criminal enterprise, is responsible as a co-perpetrator and is thereby liable for the crimes committed in the camp during the entirety of its existence. And that concludes my submissions, unless, of course, Your Honours have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Ms. Brady, I just want to be clear in my mind as to the Prosecution's submission regarding maybe one of the factors, differentiating liability under the provisions of Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). My understanding of your submission, especially when discussing the activities of appellant Radic, my understanding was that for liability under Article 7(1), in a joint criminal enterprise, type 2, the one the Prosecution is submitting, it is not necessary for the Prosecution to prove a superior/subordinate relationship among those found to be participants. Am I correct in my understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly correct in your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I was interested in your last -- oh, sorry. Sorry. No, no, no. I didn't realise Judge Weinberg de Roca wanted to speak. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you. Ms. Brady, just a short question, because it sounds very effectus, but what does the meaning the Prosecution gives to "swallowed up by the darkness"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I read the transcript and saw this word, these words, I didn't myself know exactly what was meant. But the question was meant that as in nothing terribly catastrophic, nothing bad happened, right, when people left the camp. So it was in that term. It was a rather ambiguous, strange term to use. We could agree on that. But it seems that the clear impression of the question and the answer is that nothing awful would happen to people who left. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Brady. I was interested in your submission to the effect that it hasn't been shown that the Trial Chamber was not reasonable, and so on. Well, now, everybody, I take it, is familiar with the concept that an Appeals Chamber does not reverse a finding of fact by the Trial Chamber, mainly because, if it were the Trial Chamber, it would have concluded otherwise. The Appeals Chamber would have to go on to find that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have found as the Trial Chamber did. Now, do we have to take into account Mr. Fila's very interesting submission to the effect that, well, he couldn't really look the Presiding Judge in the eye and say: You are not reasonable. That's a very interesting submission. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I actually think that it might come down to an interpretation of the word "reasonableness." From Mr. Fila's response to your question, I got the understanding that perhaps in the way it has been translated, perhaps in Serbian, B/C/S, that to say that something is unreasonable is sort of like to say that it's shockingly absurd and one that sort of calls on the very integrity or character of the person who made the finding. And I don't think that that is by any means the standard which this Appeals Chamber implies. Indeed, it would be very uncomfortable for Your Honours in overturning the decisions made by your brother and sister Judges at the Trial Chamber level if that was going to be the case. It doesn't mean that. It's not sort of derogatory. It basically means that no reasonable Trial Chamber on the facts could have come to that conclusion that there is something inherently wrong about the reliability of the evidence upon which they relied or their judgement of the credibility of a witness, which is something that no fact-finder could have found. And I think I'll leave it at that and ponder it more. A very philosophical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila has raised a very interesting point, I thought. So I understand you to be saying that such a remark is not directed personally to the Judge in question, but merely to the discharge of his functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, while you're on your legs, may I ask you another question. I have myself gone backwards and forwards on this, I'm sure. So what I'm going to raise with you is a question. I'm not putting a proposition to you. And I speak subject to the control of my colleagues who are versed in the civil law system, both on the Bench and the bar. I'm talking about your reference to Rule 94(B), I think it was, and to the way the Judge notices, judicially notices, a finding of fact made by another Chamber. You mentioned a plea agreement, and I think the proposition was that that facility is inapplicable to cases involving a plea agreement because there's really no adjudication in those instances. But do we not have to bear in mind the injunction of one of your colleagues today, I think Mr. Carmona, that this Tribunal is really of a hybrid nature; we collect within the jurisprudence of the Tribunal all the trends that we see to be relevant, and more particularly, those of the civil law and the common law. Is that not something to be borne in mind when we talk of a plea agreement? My understanding is this: Sure, even in the common law system, a plea agreement doesn't result in a finding of guilt. There has to be an adjudication. The court has to find that the plea was voluntary and understood by the accused, and so on. And maybe that is the same in the case of the civil law system. But am I not right that the civil law system goes a little further in that it says: Look, a guilty plea doesn't have the kind of conclusiveness and finality that it has in the common law system. It's merely evidence upon which the court needs to make a finding. Now, if that is so, if that is so, and I speak subject to the control of more learned colleagues in the civil law system - do we not have to bear in mind this: That it seems to me that, procedurally, the Tribunal has, in this matter, followed more in the direction of the civil law system than in the common law system so that you end up with a plea agreement, which is only evidence, to be followed by a determination made by the court. Is that not an adjudication which has to be judicially noticed by another Chamber under 94(B)? I may be totally wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course you're correct about the hybrid nature of this Tribunal, and I also understand the differences that a civil law approach would take to a plea agreement in contradiction to a common law approach which basically accepts the plea and -- well, it doesn't follow it blindly, of course not; but there's less of an inquisition or real study of the evidence to make sure that everything is proven, still, with the plea of guilty just being one further fact. But I think that notwithstanding that, there is still a real issue -- no. Let me put it this way: When it comes to positive determinations or positive findings in a judgement based on a plea agreement, the Trial Chamber, of course, has to be satisfied, whether you adopt a civil or a common law approach, has to be satisfied that that murder occurred or that rape occurred, even despite -- even with the plea of guilty. It would still have to be satisfied on its own merits of the case. But I think there's a distinction when something's left out of a sentencing judgement based on a plea agreement, because there you have a lot of different factors which could have gone into the decision by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution as to what -- with the Defence, different factors influencing what's going to be part of the plea agreement. The point is that we just don't know. And this is the danger of relying on the plea agreement as a source of adjudicated facts. We don't know exactly why something, for example, was not included. All we know is that something was included, not why it was not there. And I gave the example, bringing it back to this case, that the Trial Chamber in Sikirica, we don't know why they didn't include this rape. And I think that it would be second guessing what the Trial Chamber in Sikirica was doing. What was its problem with Witness K, to put it very colloquially? Why did it reject it? Because it because of a problem with reliability of this person's evidence? And there, there were identification issues that differentiated? Or was it a substantial problem with an underlying issue related to this witness? We just don't know. And I think the dangers of relying, then, on plea agreements whether it's a civil or common law approach, I think the dangers are still there, nonetheless. And I would also say that I don't know whether the first part of Your Honour's question was also getting to another slightly different point, but that can't you, as an Appeals Chamber, why not, if this is a sort of more hybrid system, why can't you as an Appeals Chamber absorb findings made from different Trial Chambers just to take note of them? And our submission on that is: No, you have to actually go through the 94 bis procedure. Otherwise, in effect, you have an appellate structure which is a corrective procedure, in which we have one way of bringing forward new facts, additional evidence on appeal, and then all of a sudden Your Honours would be sort of saying: Well, there's a trial judgement in so-and-so which found this against this witness or there's a trial judgement in that case which found another point. So I think we have to be very careful. I don't exclude that you couldn't use adjudicated facts, but I think you'd have to adopt an equally cautious approach. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do your very interesting remarks take us in the direction of saying that such a case isn't really excluded on principle under 94(B), but it's admissible subject to a careful evaluation of the weight to be attributed to the matter? In other words, a plea agreement in our case may be taken to be more evidential than in the common law system, where it's more conclusive.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Possibly, Your Honour, but I don't see how you would overcome the basic question of how you would conduct that evaluation of the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You may well be right. I don't know. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honours. I turn to deal with mainly the factual grounds of the appellant Mr. Zigic's submissions. I say at the outset that my colleagues have dealt with the common grounds, the so-called common grounds of the four appellants so comprehensively and thoroughly that there is very little if anything I can add to the appellant Mr. Zigic's common grounds. It is important when dealing with Mr. Zigic's appeal to set out, or to remind the parties, and again, of course, the Appeals Chamber, of the standard of an appeal and what the Appeals Chamber is actually doing in hearing Mr. Zigic's appeal. And we remind the Appeals Chamber that -- and Mr. Zigic's counsel, that mere dissatisfaction with the factual findings of a Trial Chamber is just not a valid basis for an appeal. An appellant -- and here Mr. Zigic must identify the error of fact of which they complain. And the appellant must establish that this error was critical, vital, to the verdict. And the error of fact has to be such that it occasions a miscarriage of justice, such to attract the Appeals Chamber's intervention to overturn a finding and a verdict. That, of course, as Your Honours are aware, comes from the Kunarac Appeals Chamber at paragraph 39. And it goes without saying that this, of course, isn't a retrial, and repetition of arguments and submissions made and lost at trial doesn't constitute an appeal. Repetition of those arguments, or asking for a reconsideration of the evidence, is what we call a de novo hearing, in this case would be on the depositions, on the papers, on the evidence before the Trial Chamber. But it's not an appeal. Of course, the Trial Chamber, as the trier of facts, is in the best position to assess and weigh the evidence. The evidence is extensively heard. And I quote here from Kunarac, at paragraph 39, adopting the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber's decision at paragraph 30, and I quote it in full: "The Appeals Chamber therefore gives a margin of deference to the findings of facts reached by a Trial Chamber. It is only where the evidence relied upon by the Trial Chamber would not have been accepted by any reasonable tribunal of fact or where the evaluation of the evidence is 'wholly erroneous' may the Appeals Chamber substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber." Now, I quote this in full because having heard the appellant's submissions, and especially the oral ones yesterday, it appears to the Prosecution that an attempt is being made to re-ventilate most of the issues or many of the issues which were argued and lost at trial. And of course, that is impermissible before this Chamber. The Trial Chamber, of course, heard all the witnesses, heard the questioning from all parties and all parties had an extensive opportunity to cross-examine. And in fact the record reveals that the Trial Chamber itself enthusiastically stepped in on many occasions and conducted quite extensive questioning of many of the witnesses. The Trial Chamber of course evaluated the evidence it heard and then it came to a lengthy and well-reasoned decision, a decision, in our submission, which must stand. In submissions yesterday, Mr. Stojanovic, counsel for Mr. Zigic, made what we could only describe, or as it seems to be, some political arguments. Now, we of course - and we understand the Appeals Chamber will of course disregard these - but he seemed to be saying basically, or implying, that the Croats and the Muslims brought on themselves what happened at Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje by failing to vote to stay in Yugoslavia. The reason for this apparent submission seems to be some attempt to redefine persecution away from Article 5 of the Statute, because Mr. Stojanovic then went on to say, basically, that persecution on a political basis is a milder form of persecution and seemed to be implying that, well, it may be okay afterwards; and after all, this is what you get for not voting to remain in Yugoslavia. Of course, I remind the Appeals Chamber that Article 5 forbids persecution on grounds of race, religion, and politics, and there's no argument about any of them having a higher or lesser role in the calendar of persecution. And in any event, the persecution in the Prijedor region, and specifically in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, was, of course, based upon all three. And in the Prosecution's submission, it is neither possible nor desirable to attempt to separate them out. Now, the appellant Mr. Zigic was of course convicted of his significant contribution to the horrific crimes committed at Omarska detention camp in Prijedor in 1992. The complaint yesterday in oral submissions appeared to be, at one point, that the indictment contained allegations over this three-month period. Well, yes, it did. And the Trial Chamber made well-reasoned, specific findings relating to crimes committed on different days during the period between the 24th of May and the 30th of August, 1992. The findings the Trial Chamber made related to various incidents which occurred between the end of May and early April - sorry - early August 1992. There is nothing impermissible about this charging practice. It is completely normal. And if you were charging a joint criminal enterprise, we see no other way in which you can do it other than to name the closed period in which the Prosecution alleges that it occurred. Ms. Rashid earlier today submitted, very, very comprehensively on the meaning of joint criminal enterprise, and in particular, the second variation from the Tadic Appeals decision. Yesterday, Mr. Stojanovic's submissions on behalf of the appellant Mr. Zigic -- I did have some difficulty understanding exactly where he was going. He made a complaint about the judgement. He said elucidating the concept of a joint criminal enterprise in "an extremely incoherent and contradictory and inadmissible way. It is our firm impression that the Trial Chamber understood this concept as a separate act which we must point out does not exist in the Statute or the Tribunal." Though I won't trespass over the grounds Ms. Brady and Ms. Rashid have already comprehensively dealt with, I just raise that because, as with most of the grounds which the appellant Mr. Zigic puts forward before this Chamber, he doesn't really state coherently what the alleged error was that the Trial Chamber made. It seems to be -- the interpretation we make of this, it appears to be on the Defence case, they say Mr. Zigic was in Omarska for only half an hour on one day. Therefore, the Trial Chamber's error must have been in finding a separate act which doesn't exist in the Statute of the Tribunal. That's what we think it means. However, if the Trial Chamber found against Mr. Zigic on this most important part, that is, when he was in Omarska, for how long and what he did there, as it did, the appellant Mr. Zigic must lose on this point unless he can demonstrate error. Moving to his specific role in the joint criminal enterprise. This was a systematic joint criminal enterprise, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 323(c) of its judgement: A joint criminal enterprise, a facility to ... discriminate against and otherwise abuse non-Serbs from Prijedor, which functioned as a means to rid the territory of or subjugate non-Serbs." The Trial Chamber went on at paragraph 324, specifically in relation to Mr. Zigic's knowledge and hence the mens rea in his contribution: "Anyone regularly working in or visiting Omarska camp would have had to know that the crimes were widespread throughout the camp." Now, once the Trial Chamber has found that Mr. Zigic was in that category, that is, a person who was regularly working in or visiting Omarska camp. Here, of course, it is regularly visiting. The issue then moves to the significance of that person's contribution to the system. That is the basis of liability, as Ms. Rashid emphasised in her learned submissions this morning. And of course, this is particularly so in a systematic form of joint criminal enterprise, such as in a persecutory detention camp. In this system, the crimes are of course relevant to establish the existence of a system of persecution. And here, in this particular case, the Trial Chamber was entitled to use and did in fact use Mr. Zigic's crimes that he committed in Omarska to find that this system of persecution existed. Now, this, of course -- the appellant's argument all falls down, of course, if the Trial Chamber found, as it was perfectly entitled to do, that he was there for more than half an hour on one particular day. And, as Ms. Rashid emphasised this morning, the duration of a person's contributions does not necessarily determine the significance of their contribution. The crimes which the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Zigic committed at Omarska were significant within that particular joint criminal enterprise to persecute. The crimes were such and so significant that they would have been significant in any similar joint criminal enterprise. As Ms. Rashid pointed out and as I emphasise here, such a joint criminal enterprise relies upon people like Mr. Zigic. It relies upon murderers, it relies upon torturers. A joint criminal enterprise to persecute, operating as a means to rid the territory, rid the territory, as the Trial Chamber found, or subjugate non-Serbs relies on that level of fear and oppression and people like Mr. Zigic perpetrating it. But again, Ms. Rashid touched on this this morning, as in any joint criminal enterprise to persecute, the participant does not need to know of each crime committed. Indeed, in a system, or systematic form of joint criminal enterprise, such as in a detention camp, they could not - sorry. I said systematic. I meant systemic. I've been corrected by my colleagues. In a systemic system of joint criminal enterprise, a participant could not know of every possible crime committed, such as the nature of a 24-hour camp. The participant only requires the knowledge that a wide variety of crimes were being committed, and that was knowledge which Mr. Zigic had to have, based upon his regular visits to and activities in Omarska and, importantly, what he did there. And of course, we must not lose sight of the fact that at the same time he was doing this in Omarska he was also doing identical things to sometimes the same victims in Keraterm, just up the road. If we go to the level of his participation or the visits, and if we go to the complaint that he was only there for half an hour one day, and look at the Trial Chamber's findings, apart from the specific findings regarding Becir Medjunjanin and Witness T, which occurred on about the 11th or 12th of June, 1992, the Trial Chamber also found that he committed torture on the 10th of June against AJ, Asef Kapetanovic, and AK. But in addition to that evidence of those witnesses and the corroborating witnesses as to his activities on those particular days, the Trial Chamber also heard evidence from a witness Azedin Oklopcic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And this was at page 1900 of the transcript, and it was indeed in answer to a question by my learned colleague Mr. Stojanovic asking how often Mr. Zigic would come to Omarska, to which the answer was: Mr. Zigic, Timarac and Dusko Knezevic would come to the Omarska camp and stay in the Omarska camp together. Mr. Stojanovic persisted: How many times did you see Zigic in the Omarska camp, he asked. The answer on the following page, 1901, was: "At least ten times, and two or three times at Trnopolje." The witness went on: "Let me tell you. It was an attraction when Zigic, Timarac, and Dusko turned up, because they knew at the time when they turned up they would see something they wouldn't even see on film. And when it happened that Zigic beat Rezak or Began or anyone else, all the other guards from the surrounding points would come up to watch, to experience those incidents." The Trial Chamber had clear and compelling and cogent evidence before it of Mr. Zigic's regular and repeated and eager visits to the Omarska detention camp. Still on JCE, physical or direct perpetration of a serious crime that advances the goal of a criminal enterprise would constitute a significant contribution. Now, that's what the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 309. The respondent here says the Trial Chamber made no error after hearing all the evidence in coming to that finding, and the appellant has demonstrated no error. Zigic's contributions were significant, because he contributed directly to the core crimes in the common design, that was to persecute the non-Serbs. And this goes directly to the mens rea, the requisite discriminatory intention, and as to whether he's an aider and abettor or a co-perpetrator. The example Ms. Rashid gave this morning of an individual walking into Omarska, acquainting himself with the climate of impunity, and on one occasion perhaps maliciously and deliberately killing someone, her submission was that the contribution could be so direct and significant to furthering the joint criminal enterprise that the only inference available would be that the person agreed with the system. With Mr. Zigic, of course, it goes much further. You have murder, you have torture, you have beatings, and you have repeated visits. The Trial Chamber was entitled to find, as it did at paragraph 610, that Zigic made a significant contribution and was a significant participant in his -- and that he, "Aggressively and eagerly participated in the persecution of non-Serbs in Omarska." The Prosecution emphasises that this degree of participation was eager, it was regular, it was voluntary; indeed, enthusiastic. And further, on the issue of mens rea, and although the Trial Chamber didn't do this, there's no reason, in principle, why it could not have used the evidence of his persecutory crimes at Keraterm or Trnopolje in the same period pleaded in the indictment to corroborate the significance of his contribution to the joint criminal enterprise to persecute at Omarska. The Trial Chamber made no error in finding his discriminatory intent based upon his abuse of the non-Serbs, the ethnic slurs which were accompanied by extreme violence, and the repetition of them shows mens rea and discriminatory intention.
