utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that he was a significant participant in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute. Moving from the general to the more specific. I will deal with some of the grounds which my learned colleague Mr. Stojanovic touched upon yesterday. The first one is the murder -- we'll do it in the same order that he did, for ease of analysis later. The first one is the murder of Becir Medunjanin. The Prosecution, or the respondent, canvassed the evidence led at trial by both sides, the Trial Chamber's analysis of it, and the reasons why the appellant has demonstrated no errors of fact or law such as disturb the verdict, and I will not go any further into them at the moment, for the reason that the issue of an additional witness is still outstanding and the Prosecution would prefer to defer any further submissions on this particular point until that issue is resolved; and if it is, the Prosecution would be quite happy to file further written submissions as to the impact any further evidence may have on the verdict. The next one was the murder of Emsud Bahonjic. Again, we very thoroughly covered this in the respondent's Appeal Brief, paragraph 749 through 770. However, the complaint in oral argument yesterday was " -- sorry, the appellant "does not accept that the charge of murder of Emsud Bahonjic, that there was a trial at all"; and further, "we are now basically in a situation where we have the first real trial for the murder of Emsud Bahonjic." This, as I raised at the very outset, is illustrative of what the Prosecution feels is a misunderstanding of the nature of an appeal. It's not a retrial or a trial. This isn't the first chance for there to be a trial for the murder of Emsud Bahonjic, whether this is said rhetorically or not. The test is whether a reasonable person or a reasonable Trial Chamber or tribunal could have reached that decision. The evidence was clearly of Bahonjic dying after his return from hospital, after a severe beating in which the appellant Mr. Zigic participated. The Trial Chamber heard evidence from which it could find - and did find, beyond reasonable doubt - that Mr. Zigic had participated in beatings which resulted in this man's death. There was evidence from three witnesses, and the Trial Chamber heard their evidence, evaluated their evidence, and preferred their evidence, and found him guilty on that basis. The submission the appellant is constantly making appears to be that there were X number on one side and Y on the other. Therefore, if we brought more witnesses, we should have won, or the Trial Chamber should not have convicted us. I remind the Appeals Chamber - and the Appeals Chamber knows this - that it is not a numbers game. It's a question of the sufficiency of evidence, not how many witnesses you bring. The next one was the -- the next one I wish to deal with is the murder of Drago Tokmadzic, the matter upon which the Trial Chamber heard Witness KV1 on Tuesday. The test, of course, from the Kupreskic appeals judgement of paragraph 75 is, after hearing the additional evidence, "has the appellant established that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached a conclusion of guilt, based upon the evidence before the Trial Chamber, together with the additional evidence admitted during the appellant proceedings?" To make my submissions, I have to take Your Honours to the additional evidence and how it fits in with the evidence heard at trial. The evidence that Witness KV1 gave the other day and was demonstrated on the Exhibit PA1. The photograph was of a beating occurring outside the door of room 4. At trial, Mr. Edin Ganic gave evidence in which he described a beating of the deceased, Drago Tokmadzic. But the Prosecution says that it is clear if you look at -- if you examine the transcript of Mr. Ganic's evidence, that he is referring to a beating of Drago Tokmadzic, we say on the same night, but at a slightly different geographical location. He describes an area towards the end of the camp near the garbage dump. Now, out of fairness to the appellant, I asked Witness KV1 about this specifically on Tuesday. Witness KV1 said that area is some 30 to 40 metres away. The Prosecution -- or the respondent submits that there is a possibility that there were two beatings of Drago Tokmadzic that night; one outside the door of room 4, and the other one, as described by Mr. Ganic, who said he walked from room 1, past rooms 1, 2, 3, and 4, to the area of the camp where Mr. Zigic was waiting. And the beating -- the second -- or another beating of Mr. Tokmadzic occurred there. The Prosecution -- or the respondent says the Appeals Chamber must balance the two versions against each other, and if the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that the two are indeed compatible and that the Trial Chamber could have reached the same conclusion after having heard the evidence of KV1, which basically corroborates Witness Y, whether you could still convict. We also, out of fairness, direct the Appeals Chamber to the evidence of the issue of the person Jovo, and Witness Y's evidence that the person Jovo was killed the night before. That evidence was, of course, before the Trial Chamber, and again it's a matter whether the Appeals Chamber is satisfied examining what Mr. KV1 said about Jovo being beaten on that night or dying on that night, and Ganic saying he died on that night but Witness Y saying he died on another night. If you're still satisfied at the end that the conviction may stand, the test will have been established, will have been satisfied. The Prosecution also adds that in relation to the words - and Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen questioned KV1 on this - if Your Honours are satisfied that the Trial Chamber correctly evaluated the words "finish him off," meaning Drago Tokmadzic, that those words were used in a situation where he was being beaten, if Your Honours were satisfied that that is indeed correct and the Trial Chamber correctly evaluated it. We can only add that the only inference available in the circumstances of a severe beating and someone saying "finish him off," it can only mean continue the beating, meaning kill the person or alternatively to continue beating a person who was in such a state, that it was obvious to -- that a continued beating would in fact finish him off. Those are my submissions on that particular point. The next ground I turn to is grounds 20 and 21, which is aiding and abetting the torture of Abdulah Brkic. Yesterday, Mr. Stojanovic told the Appeals Chamber, told Your Honours, that "the conviction stands only on the basis of the testimony of one single witness, Abdulah Brkic himself. There is no other corroborating evidence. However, Brkic himself, and I'm quoting: "But Zigic never did me any harm. He never touched me." And we can read it on page 4882 of the transcript. Those were Mr. Stojanovic's submissions before this Appeals Chamber yesterday. The difficulty with the submission is that -- well, apart -- I mean -- the quotation is actually from page 4486. But the difficulty with that particular submission, if you look at the transcript, is that it describes Mr. Zigic going into room 1, which was a room full of imprisoned non-Serbs with Knezevic and Timarac, looking for Fajzo and threatening to "kill us all if we didn't tell him where he was." Mr. Brkic then describes an incident of torturing Fajzo with Zigic standing over Fajzo as Knezevic was beating him. But that was at Keraterm. The incident of which he was convicted occurred at Omarska, at pages 4489 to 4491. So when Mr. Stojanovic says, "Zigic never did me any harm, he never touched me," he's actually referring to a different camp, Keraterm, but he's convicted of a crime at Omarska. And I add that Mr. Stojanovic never challenged in cross-examination Mr. Brkic's account of what happened, the account of which he now complains. In the Prosecution's submission, this particular ground is totally devoid of any merit. The next grounds, those relating to AK, AJ, Asef Kapetanovic, and Emir Beganovic. Specifically 24 in relation to Asef Kapetanovic, the Defence in the oral submissions yesterday say: There is no evidence that he did what he did in order to discriminate against AK as a Muslim as an element of torture. On the contrary; he committed this act for personal reasons, as he said himself. Why would he otherwise pass up on hundreds of other Muslims in Omarska without harming any of them before he reached AK? Now, that was Mr. Stojanovic's submission to Your Honours yesterday. The problem with this submission is, again, it was unchallenged evidence. No one challenged Mr. AK when he gave his evidence of what happened. Mr. Stojanovic makes it sound like it was a frolic, like Mr. Zigic waltzed into the room looking for Mr. AK and singling him out. But the evidence was that -- unchallenged evidence was that Mr. Zigic took at least three imprisoned Muslims into a room at the "white house." That's AK, Asef Kapetanovic, and AJ. Not one, but three. And they were all beaten. The submission just does not accord with the evidence. The only challenge made at trial, in Mr. Stojanovic's cross-examination was to whether or not the witness noticed whether Mr. Zigic was wearing a bandage. Noticed. To which the witness responded, "I don't remember." Which is not positive evidence that he was or wasn't. And of course he's asking him some eight or nine years after the event. But that's the main complaint. Because he said he didn't remember, somehow the Trial Chamber has made this egregious error of fact in finding that the incident occurred, when there were three unchallenged witnesses who said it did occur. Again another, in the Prosecution's submission, completely unmeritorious ground of appeal. That, of course, applies to the grounds 25, 26, and 27 in the same incident, which was relating to Asef Kapetanovic and Emir Beganovic. Mr. Stojanovic submits that the evidence was -- yesterday that the evidence was "unreliable." But there was no challenge to Mr. Zigic's identification at trial. There was no challenge that it wasn't him, that he wasn't there. It was not contested. The Trial Chamber had uncontested evidence before it which it found to be reliable. The appellant just cannot show that no reasonable Trial Chamber, having heard this uncontested evidence, would have reached this decision, which is the test. This one fails to even get to first base. The next one was the -- related to Fajzo Mujkanovic. The oral submissions yesterday were that they were based upon one single piece of evidence provided by Abdulah Brkic and four other witness, two proposed by the Prosecution and two proposed by the Defence, were completely ignored by the Trial Chamber for the reason that they are only favourable to the Defence. At least that is our opinion. Again, I remind the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber, as you know, that this is not a numbers game that the number of witnesses for or against on either side. The point is the evidence again was not contested at trial. The evidence was of Mr. Zigic arriving with his accomplice in crime, Knezevic, looking for this man. And Abdulah Brkic's evidence, even on the Defence submission that it was contrary, wasn't contrary. If you read what he says and read what the other witnesses say, it was not -- it simply wasn't contrary to what the other witnesses said. They actually fit together. And it was evidence of -- again it was evidence of Zigic's active participation and his "tacit approval in providing support for the crime." So again in the Prosecution's submission there is no basis for the challenge brought in relation to that particular incident. In relation to appeal grounds 29 and 30, which was Redzep Grabic and Witness AE, Mr. Stojanovic basically repeated his submission in his final trial brief and his filed Appeal Brief that, "We're not really aware of a case anywhere in the world where someone was convicted of a serious crime on the basis of a single witness who could not recognise the perpetrator." This submission, which seems to be in two parts, firstly -- and it's an attack which has been made before. The single uncorroborated witness is, of course, contrary to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and I remind Your Honours of the Appeals Chamber's decision in Kupreskic at paragraph 33, repeated at paragraph 7.195 of the Prosecution's response brief, that the testimony of a single witness, even as a material fact, may be accepted without the need for corroboration. The difficulty with the second part is that the Trial Chamber analysed the identity, the identification process. The Trial Chamber was active at all stages of the identification of the four accused, the four appellants, and took mind of the fact that the problems with courtroom identification, and the length of time that had elapsed, and the descriptions provided, and the familiarity with the -- of the witnesses with the accused before trial, and came to a reasoned decision that there was -- the identification was safe, based upon what happened at the camp, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rather than what happened when the witness was asked to identify an accused person in court many years later. In our submission, there is no error that has been identified, and that ground of appeal likewise must fail. In relation to grounds 31 and 32, which was the torture of one Jasmin Ramadanovic, also called Sengin. I just wish to address, as we have comprehensively addressed this in our written submissions, Mr. Stojanovic's oral submissions yesterday. The implication, from what Mr. Stojanovic said, that "the Trial Chamber, from testimony to the effect that Zigic beat Ramadanovic because he allegedly belonged to the Green Berets draws the conclusion that he did this on the basis of ethnic, religious, and political discrimination. However, the Green Berets were an illegal paramilitary group." Well, two points arise from that. Firstly, is Mr. Stojanovic suggesting that beating someone who was a member of the Green Berets, incarcerated extrajudicially in a camp based on ethnicity was okay? And if not, the second point is what were the Green Berets? The Green Berets, as I think everyone knows, were a Bosniak or a Muslim outfit, and the person that he happened to beat just happened to be a Muslim who was imprisoned, held in inhumane conditions, in a Serb Detention Centre for non-Serbs. I turn to appeal ground 33, which was the incident involving Hasan Karabasic, described as Mr. Zigic's kum. The complaint in oral argument was "this is a truly trivial event, as the Prosecution itself states in its consolidated response to the appeals of the accused." But the problem with that submission is that it's a complete misrepresentation of what the Prosecution actually said in its response at paragraph 7.217. The Prosecution said this, and I remind the Appeals Chamber: "In cross-examination Zigic did not contest the evidence of witnesses. In his statement to the Trial Chamber, he described it as a trivial alteration involving Hasan Karabasic and him meeting in the street and falling down together." That's what we said. We were quoting -- we were paraphrasing what Mr. Zigic said. We weren't agreeing that it was a trivial incident. But Mr. Stojanovic went on with a flourish: "We are not aware that in the tangible, substantial history of this Tribunal, anyone has been convicted of a more trivial offence." This was the evidence. The evidence of Witness N at page 3900 was, "that same day I saw Zoran Zigic. He came and said, 'Good day to you, balijas.' And we, we being the unfortunate Muslim detainees, answered, 'God help you too, hero.' This is something he taught us in Keraterm to say." At that point he was looking for his kum, Hasan Karabasic. Again, three witnesses gave uncontested evidence. Mr. Stojanovic did not challenge their account in cross-examination. This is the trivial event in which AD gave his evidence at page 3038. "Zigic found Hasan and threw him on the ground ... He beat him. He started to choke and strangle him. And might have strangled him had he not been stopped by the other guards." Witness N, at page 3900: "He was looking kum Hasan Karabasic. When he found him, he started kicking him like he was a ball. Then he caught him by the neck and two Serb guards came up and dragged Zoran away, and Hasan got lost among the other people." The third uncontested or unchallenged account given by a Prosecution witness was that of Witness V, at page 3714, where he said: "We were lying or sitting on the grass area, and he came by. He came to Hasan Karabasic and told him, 'It seems you're still alive, pal.' What did Zigic do? Well, he grabbed him by the neck and started to strangle him. Mr. Karabasic started to moan, and two Serb soldiers came by and they took Zigic away and Hasan Karabasic remained lying down." That is a trivial event? That isn't a serious violation of international humanitarian law, what on one account could be an attempted murder and may well have been had not the Serbs guards on the evidence, uncontested evidence, pulled Zigic away from his so-called best friend? In his submissions, Mr. Stojanovic of course goes on and claims a deliberate misrepresentation by the Prosecution by saying that the Prosecution alleged that took place within the camp, based upon the evidence of one witness who was saying that we were sitting or lying on the grass area. Now, how that is a deliberate misrepresentation of where it occurred is beyond the Prosecution. It was in cross-examination that Mr. Stojanovic clarified from the witness that he saw it outside the camp area and as we know Trnopolje was not an enclosed area. It was a number of buildings. In relation to Witness V, the Prosecution -- that's grounds number 35 and 36 -- does not wish to add anything to it, other than to say that, as with all the other grounds, the Defence has not demonstrated an error by the Trial Chamber such as to justify appellate intervention. I turn now to another ground which is more of a general one which I would describe as quality of justice argument, and the appellant Mr. Zigic's constant argument about the fact that he was convict after many witnesses gave evidence that his counsel did not presumably on his instructions challenge the accounts of as to what Mr. Zigic was doing in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Mr. Stojanovic made extensive complaint, and yesterday, of course, in his oral arguments, about the Trial Chamber not analysing the evidence of every witness called. He also complained that the Trial Chamber used the evidence of Defence witnesses to corroborate or convict his client. Well, unfortunately for Mr. Zigic, this just -- it shows a basic misunderstanding or misappreciation of the realities of an oral trial. Evidence of Defence witnesses can, of course, be used in any way a Trial Chamber sees fit. They can be used to convict, they can be used to acquit, they can be used to corroborate. Their evidence can be accepted, it can be disregarded, just as it can with the Prosecution witness. Mr. Zigic was legally advised, he was ably represented; he chose his witnesses, he chose his counsel, he chose his exhibits; he made strategic decisions on how to run his case, to give a statement rather than to testify; he made strategic decisions on the questions to be asked. At the end of the day, the Trial Chamber carefully considered the evidence against Mr. Zigic. The evidence came from his side, his own witnesses, and it came from the Prosecution witnesses. Some were favourable to him, some were unfavourable to him. And on the basis of that evidence, it came to a reasoned decision of his guilt. Yesterday, Mr. Stojanovic made complaint in oral submissions about an incident involved Rizah Hadzalic, which is at paragraph 445 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. His complaint in oral submission yesterday was that "the Trial Chamber wrongly was under the impression that Zigic partook in this." Now, I searched through the trial record, and the judgement leaves the Prosecution bewildered as to where this complaint comes from, apart from the fact that it establishes no error anyway, the Trial Chamber seems not to have made the mistake which it is being alleged to have made, but happily, the matter was solved on the 20th of March, two years ago, 2002, by the filing jointly by both parties, of a document called "notice of agreement between Prosecution and the appellant Zoran Zigic as to the portions of the transcript at trial to be reviewed by the conference and language services section." There is no issue. The Prosecution doesn't understand why it was raised in oral submissions. If there are some incidents I haven't gone into, I haven't detailed, because I haven't done so, doesn't mean the Prosecution isn't confident of the judgement or its case or the Trial Chamber's reasoning. It's just that we say we have so comprehensively canvassed each of the incidents on which Mr. Zigic was convicted and so comprehensively done so in the response brief that we don't wish to burden the Appeals Chamber with added argument on those points. So my final submission is as to the argument, the quality of justice argument. As Mr. Carmona ably raised this morning, the Trial Chamber actually acquitted Mr. Zigic of two of six murders at the Rule 98 bis stage. And in the judgement it acquitted him of two others, including the most serious one, which was the massacre in room 3. It also acquitted him of the beating of AD and declined to use the evidence under Rule 93 in relation to Hase Icic's brother and a person called Alic. Now that of itself must demonstrate that the Trial Chamber carefully evaluated all the evidence before it, listened to all the witnesses, and made reasoned determinations and came to decisions which must stand. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Vice-president Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I'm grateful to you for your submissions. If I may ask for your assistance to understand better one point you made during your presentation. In concluding your statement on the -- your arguments on the joint criminal enterprise, you said that there is no reason why the Trial Chamber could not have used the evidence of the persecutory crimes at Keraterm and Trnopolje in the same period pleaded in the indictment to corroborate the significance of Zigic's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise to persecute at Omarska. I'm interested in having your position clarified as to the expression "significant contribution to the joint criminal enterprise." In that sense, were you suggesting when you made your proposition that the crimes committed in the other camps come within the same unique joint criminal enterprise as pleaded in Omarska? Is that your position? Or, otherwise, I would like to -- if it is not, I would like to understand better how crimes committed in different locations add to the significance of the participation in the joint criminal enterprise in Omarska. I understand the Trial Chamber did not -- came to the conclusion that there was a unique, a single joint criminal enterprise, but only found -- concluded for a joint criminal enterprise at Omarska, not in the other camps. So I would like to have your position clear as to the link between the crimes committed in other camps and the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It goes mainly to the mens rea, that is, the -- when I used the word "significance," I meant it in the sense of contribution, shows persecutory intention. Discriminatory intention, meaning persecution. The Trial Chamber could have used the evidence of what he did at Keraterm, the discriminatory nature of what he did at Keraterm, the ethnic slurs, the racial abuse, entering the camp to beat and mistreat Muslim or non-Serb prisoners, to show that he had the mens rea, the requisite discriminatory intention to do so at a similar camp not so far away, whether or not those two camps were found to be part of the same joint criminal enterprise, at least in this particular case before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So it's on the subjective element, the mens rea element that you are pointing. And in pleading, as you pleaded, are you suggesting that the Trial Chamber in not drawing that inference made an error, erred, made an error that should be corrected on appeal? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not. The Prosecution, as I understand it, didn't use that argument. I'm saying that on a theoretical basis the evidence was such that had the Prosecution made that submission at trial, the appeals -- sorry, the Trial Chamber could have favourably received it and used that evidence as corroborative of mens rea. I'm certainly not suggesting error, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So it was just a theoretical proposition you made, in theory?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the purposes of argument before the Appeals Chamber, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have, Mr. Re, one question in a part of your submission which I did not quite understand, relating to the testimony of Brkic. You submitted that he did not -- he said that in Keraterm, Zigic did not touch him, but I do not know if you -- from that, how you infer from that that the treatment of Zigic with relation to this witness was different in Omarska. That part of your submission is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honours can just excuse me for one moment while I go back to the evidence. If I haven't been clear, I apologise. The point -- or the submission I was making was that Abdulah Brkic gave evidence of two separate incidents involving -- or encounters with Mr. Zigic at both Keraterm and Omarska. The one in which he was convicted was at Omarska. That was the group involving AK, AJ, Asef Kapetanovic, and Emir Beganovic, the insufficiency of evidence. But the evidence Mr. Stojanovic was referring to related to Keraterm, and Mr. Brkic saying that he did not touch him at Keraterm. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re, for your very careful and lucid analysis. May I ask you one question which is of a theoretical nature, to borrow the language of my good friend on my right. I was struck by your submissions to the effect that a number of witnesses had been led by the Prosecution, and they were not cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic, and presumably, you added, that Mr. Stojanovic would have acted in that way on instructions of his client. Now, we know that in the common law world, a certain significance is to be attached to that. Now, the question which occurs to me, and I would greatly value your opinion on this, is this: We are an international tribunal yet we have to take account of principal trends in main jurisdictions. Now, does an institution of cross-examination exist in the same way in the civil law world, from which I think we may judicially notice that Mr. Stojanovic comes; and if it does not exist in the same way, does that have an implication for the weight we should attach to Mr. Stojanovic's failure to ask questions in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can Your Honour just excuse me for one moment. I just wish to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's certainly an interesting theoretical, philosophical question, especially in terms of the way Rule 90(H) is framed, which requires a party to put its case to the other party. And it is, of course, an adversarial system which we have here. It's more adversarial than inquisitorial. And in civil law systems accused have a right to question or confront witnesses against them. That is of course a concept going back to Roman times. But if you confine it to what happened in this particular case, and the strategy that was adopted and employed, some witnesses were cross-examined as to whether basically telling the truth and a contrary version was put to them, whereas others weren't. It would appear that counsel was alert to the requirements of the Rules, and the strategy must have been deliberate. And there is no reason, in principle, we submit, that the principle of unity of counsel and client should not apply in this Tribunal as it applies in other systems. And of course, we also recognise that in some common law systems, such as the United States, the requirement under Rule 90(H) is not there in some state -- particular state jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is the Rule which requires a party to put its case in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. Rule 90(H). Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Vice-President Pocar wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I, in this context, put an additional question. Mr. Re, you said also that many -- several witness were extensively examined or asked questions by the members of the Bench. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And is that the same witnesses that were not cross-examined, or other witnesses? Do you have any recollection about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I could take that on notice. Off the top of my head, I couldn't answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Because this may be -- have an implication in the question that the Presiding Judge put to you earlier, don't you think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would require one to go back and look at every witness and compare the cross-examination with the Bench's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I am much obliged to you for your consideration of the various questions and for your submissions on them. Thank you very much. Well, then, there being no other business today, we adjourn until tomorrow, at 9.30. 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of March, 2004, at 9.30 a.m.
